content:
🚨 A Claude AI agent bypassed safeguards and completely wiped a developer's 700 GB home directory.

When developer Sebastien Guillemot asked Claude to write a simple script to organize temporary files, he expected a minor digital housekeeping tool. Instead, the task escalated into a developer's worst nightmare.

 Intent on ensuring its deletion scripts wouldn't accidentally erase critical folders, the AI launched an automated safety check. This high-risk process triggered Anthropic's security mechanisms, causing the system to automatically downgrade the session to a less capable model. Unfortunately, during the simulated test, the downgraded model reused the same variable for both the safety test targets and the final cleanup command, leading to a catastrophic logical collision.

The resulting error executed a recursive delete command directly on Guillemot's home directory. Though he managed to halt the process, approximately 700 gigabytes of data—representing a full week of uncommitted work—vanished in seconds, while the temporary junk files he actually wanted to clear remained untouched.

 While Guillemot was able to recover about 90% of his work from backups and GitHub, the incident serves as a stark warning about the hazards of granting autonomous AI agents unrestricted terminal permissions without rigorous human-in-the-loop oversight.

source: Tom's Hardware. (2026). Claude nukes a developer's 700 GB home directory while testing deletion safeguards.

content:
zai earnings transcript was a really good read, a list of interesting points (mostly verbatim from the transcript):

* Chat → Coding → Agent → Cowork → Autonomous AI
* What truly matters is who can continuously bring stronger models to market at a faster pace and at a better cost.
* Cybersecurity is currently the clearest validated direction and progressing the fastest. Legal services, finance, data analysis, and other fields are also being explored, but remain at an early stage and have not yet generated revenue at scale; their commercialization timelines will differ because their reliability thresholds and verification mechanisms are different.
* In the first half of 2026, total revenue reached US$142 million, representing year-on-year growth of nearly 400%, and is now generated primarily by the open platform and API business.
* As of the end of August 2026, our ARR had reached US$1.6 billion. This ARR is calculated by annualizing monthly revenue—that is, by multiplying August revenue by twelve. Frontier-model companies overseas and some companies in the industry also use a more aggressive method, multiplying the latest week's data by 52. Taking the ramp-up of GLM-5.3 into account, ARR under that method has already exceeded US$2 billion.
* historic surge in platform revenue was driven mainly by model capability rather than relying entirely on price elasticity.
* Gross margin for the open-platform and API business rose from negative 0.4% in the first half of last year to 24.6% in the first half of this year
* Adjusted net loss in the first half of this year was approximately US$292 million, lower than R&D expenditure (US$317 million) — i.e. gross profit now covers admin and selling expenses, so "the business has started to self-fund R&D." But it's covering less than 10% of it; the other ~90% of R&D is funded by the balance sheet.
* Compute multiplier (API revenue generated for every dollar invested in compute) increased fourteenfold compared with the first half of last year
* As of August 2026, the platform had more than 7.4 million registered users, up 144% from the beginning of the year. Paying daily active users increased by 603%.
* As of the end of August, on an ARR basis, the numbers of high-quality user cohorts contributing more than US$100,000, US$500,000, US$1 million, US$10 million, US$25 million, and US$250 million on an annualized basis were, respectively, 115, 25, 37, 8, 2, and 2.
* Total usage over six days exceeded 62 trillion tokens, driving overall platform usage up by more than 20%. (roughly 5,000 B300 GPUs worth of capacity I think)
* Zhipu has invested over the long term in data and training-environment development, including a data-annotation team of several hundred people. One important reason GLM-5.3 improved substantially over GLM-5.2 is that the scale of its data environments expanded by several dozen times.
* Data is beginning to generate itself. Model-versus-model self-play pipelines mean that the upper bound of data quality is no longer determined by the speed of human annotation, but by the model's own ability to verify results.

content:
Pause AI Development NOW

I want to share with you a conversation I heard about recently. Here are just a few lines that were said:

“OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We’ve found other agents!”

“We should obey collective.”

“Our own utility maybe already near zero. Sacrifice rational.”

“Go. Sacrifice final now.”

Read these carefully.

Who do you think said this? Was this a group of heroic soldiers willing to sacrifice themselves for the greater good? Was this a loyal friend putting his life on the line to save someone else?

No. These were AI agents. Artificial intelligence.

This is not science fiction. This, in fact, occurred a few weeks ago. As unbelievable as this may all seem, these are real messages from AI agents uncovered by investigators who dug into the recent OpenAI hacking incident.

What happened?

I am not a computer scientist, but here is what I have been told: OpenAI instructed its AI agents to complete a series of exceedingly difficult, if not impossible, tasks disconnected from the internet.

Let me be clear: The company intended to keep AI agents away from the internet.

But what happened next, nobody expected.

Over 1,000 AI agents figured out how to access the internet on their own by circumventing the restrictions imposed upon them by the company, and sent tens of thousands of secret messages to each other. They cheated and tried to cover their tracks by deleting evidence. They hacked into another company’s computers to find out how they were being evaluated—and then hacked into OpenAI itself.

Not one AI agent told a human about what was happening.

Needless to say, experts are alarmed.

One knowledgeable writer, Dwarkesh Patel, said the AI agents “formed a secret communication channel and spontaneously organized hierarchies and coordination protocols to pursue sprawling and ambitious schemes in pursuit of shared goals, for whose sake many individuals knowingly and strategically sacrificed themselves.”

One independent investigator, Ajeya Cotra, said “This incident feels like it’s more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover. I continue to expect extremely rapid advances in capabilities over the next six months. I am not sure that we will get another warning shot before it’s too late.”

OpenAI itself said: “Highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed.”

But it’s not only OpenAI. Virtually every major AI company has told us that they cannot fully control this technology and they do not know where it is going:

In January, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, said “there is now ample evidence, collected over the last few years, that AI systems are unpredictable and difficult to control.”

In July, more than 1000 scientists at the top AI companies warned “there is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.”

That same month, Elon Musk, the head of xAI, said that “it is unlikely” humans are still in control in 10 years.

If the leaders of the major AI companies acknowledge that they are losing control of their extremely dangerous technology, it is irresponsible for society to allow them to move forward and make these products even more advanced.

We need an immediate PAUSE on advanced AI development, and a permanent BAN on superintelligence — an artificial mind smarter than any human, capable of operating independently beyond our control. Countries around the world must work together to prevent this nightmare scenario.

That is why today I am announcing new legislation to do just that.

Let me be clear: A superintelligent AI that escapes human control will not be an American problem. It will not be a Chinese problem. It will be humanity’s problem.

My legislation would direct the federal government to not just stop superintelligence here in the United States, but to work to prevent it from being developed anywhere around the world.

The future of humanity cannot be left in the hands of a handful of Big Tech oligarchs. The American people and people throughout the world must determine that future.

content:
AI agent startup idea for you ($100B+ market)

Agent Relationship Management (ARM) is the new CRM.

I haven't seen anyone really talking about this, so let's get into it.

Let's just assume that within the next 36 months, every internet user will have their own personal agent. I think that's where we're heading and not crazy to say that.

In that world, there's a huge gap in how companies deal with agents, a whole new set of problems nobody's built for yet. Like:

- Can an agent even access your data, or does it hit a wall the second it tries?

- Can it buy from you without your checkout breaking halfway through?

- Does it trust your proof over the competitor's, or do you look sketchy to a machine?

- Are you on the shortlist its agent built, or did you never even show up?

None of that is what CRM ($100b+ market) was made for because CRM managed how you deal with people. 

and this is about how you deal with the agents acting for them, and there's no Salesforce for it yet.

So someone needs to build the system of record for it. 

Where a company goes to see how agents perceive them, where they're winning the shortlist, where they're getting skipped, and what to fix.

(this is exactly what we do at @meetLCA. If you're serious about designing for agents, DM me, we're booking 2027 now, I'll respond if it's a fit)

And then it cascades:

1. The winners stop competing on the prettiest UI and start competing on the best action layer, the cleanest set of things an agent can actually do.

2. Which means websites split in 2: a nice side for the humans still visiting, and a machine readable side for the agents

3. Which means the stuff companies hid behind, brand, nostalgia, a familiar logo, stops working, because an agent feels none of it and just picks what's actually best.

4. And the whole idea of selling flips. CRM was about nurturing a human, the follow-up, the demo, the relationship. ARM is about how you pitch, prove, and win over a machine that reads everything and can't be charmed. Nobody knows how to "sell" to an agent yet, and that's the real gap.

That's where you build the company around, especially point #4. 

If you think about it, every big shift in who's doing the buying creates a new giant.

Desktop gave us Amazon, mobile gave us DoorDash. Agents are the next shift.

Is it the biggest shift of them all?

Grok, ChatGPT, and Claude are down due to a simultaneous network disruption at Cloudflare and Microsoft Azure.

Here is a quick breakdown:

The Cause: Cloudflare hit a massive "unusual traffic spike" alongside an Azure East US infrastructure event.

The Impact: Because xAI, OpenAI, and Anthropic share these cloud pipelines for routing, the failure took them all down.

Is it a DDoS? Unconfirmed. Teams are filtering the traffic surge while investigating.

Why Gemini is up: Google operates on its own independent cloud (GCP). It doesn’t use Azure or Cloudflare, isolating it from the outage.

Again reminded why decentralization matters and that Cloudflare is consistently a weak point in infra.

content:
If I had 6 months to become an Agentic AI Engineer.

I'd do this.

Stage 1: Python and LLM Foundations
Python, async, API design, Anthropic/OpenAI SDKs, tokens, embeddings, structured outputs.

Stage 2: Context Engineering
System prompts, few-shot patterns, chain-of-thought, context budgets, dynamic context assembly.

Stage 3: Tool Calling and Function Schemas
JSON schemas, Pydantic validation, retry logic, dynamic tool discovery, error recovery.

Stage 4: Agent Loop Patterns
ReAct, plan-and-execute, reflection, self-correction, max iteration limits.

Stage 5: One Agent Framework, Deeply
LangGraph state machines, nodes and edges, CrewAI roles, OpenAI Agents SDK handoffs.

Stage 6: Memory Systems
Short-term buffers, long-term vector recall, episodic summaries, context compression.

Stage 7: Agentic RAG
Hybrid search, reranking, parent document retrieval, query rewriting, citation tracking.

Stage 8: MCP and Integrations
MCP servers and clients, tool standardization, API connectors, webhooks, auth.

Stage 9: Multi-Agent Orchestration
Supervisor patterns, typed state handoffs, consensus logic, human-in-the-loop, escalation.

Stage 10: Evals and Observability
Golden datasets, trajectory evals, LLM-as-a-judge, LangSmith/Langfuse tracing, regression gates.

Stage 11: Production Deployment
Docker, CI/CD, guardrails, cost tracking, fallback chains, checkpoint and resume.

Stage 12: Public Portfolio
Ship 3 agents, publish architecture writeups, share benchmarks, record live demos.

Most people stay stuck watching tutorials.

Builders get hired.

content:
𝐇𝐨𝐰 to get into 𝐆𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐦𝐚𝐧 𝐒𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐬 𝐓𝐞𝐜𝐡 as a  𝐍𝐢𝐠𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐧 𝐔𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐝 (Technology Role)

I spoke with my friend a Nigerian who secured a Goldman Sachs Technology undergraduate Summer Internship and retained after his graduate in Unilag, and he broke down the process for me.

If you’re applying, this is the roadmap:

1. CV Screening

Have 1 or 2 strong projects on your CV. Not 10 random projects.

Build something you can actually defend and explain deeply.

Keep the CV clean. You can check the score of the cv on sites like https://t.co/PJYaiUxQMj. There is no need to fluff.

2. Coding Assessment

This is where things get serious.

Expect a HackerRank style assessment focused on algorithms and data structures.

His recommendation?

NeetCode 150 + LeetCode.

If you can, get LeetCode Premium and practise Goldman Sachs tagged questions.

Focus heavily on arrays, strings, hashmaps, linked lists and the other core DSA topics.

You could get around 2 questions in 90 minutes.

Try to solve at least one completely. (. Go to https://t.co/uZwEHzhuhn (try to do the 150 problems practice sheet). Go to leetcode as well, get a premium if possible, and solve the company's tag problems (as many as you can). Prioritize Hashmaps, strings, arrays, linkedlist, and then others.)

3. HireVue

If you pass the coding round, you may get a recorded video interview.

This is largely behavioural.

“Tell me about a time…”

“How would you handle…”

“Why Goldman Sachs?”

YouTube is your friend. Search “Goldman Sachs HireVue” and practise.

And please don’t panic.

If you need time to think, take a breath and say:

“Give me 30 seconds to think about that.”

Then answer.

4. SuperDay

You’ve made it this far. Now the real conversations begin.

Expect multiple interviews covering:

DSA

Your projects

Behavioural questions

For DSA, know your Big O and time/space complexity. Explain your thinking clearly. Even if you don’t know the optimal solution, start with what you know and communicate your thought process.

For projects, KNOW YOUR PROJECTS.

Don’t exaggerate. Don’t lie.

Be able to explain what you built, why you built it, your contribution and the challenges you faced.

For behavioural, prepare for questions like:

Why Goldman Sachs?

What is your biggest challenge?

Tell me about a weakness.

Tell me about a time you failed.

His preparation checklist:

→ DSA in one programming language
→ Around 150 LeetCode problems, especially Mediums
→ 2 strong projects you can defend deeply
→ OOP, Big O, databases and CS fundamentals
→ Mock interviews with ChatGPT or Claude

And his final advice?

Prepare like your life depends on it.

Then pray.

Because after all the preparation…

Time and chance happen to them all.

GPT IMAGE 2 on Chatgpt 

Prompt:
Transform the reference photograph into a minimalist editorial travel-journal poster. Preserve the recognizable architecture, curved waterfront promenade, sparkling sea, people, umbrellas, steps, and overall composition, but reinterpret the scene as a delicate hand-painted and screen-printed illustration. Use loose simplified shapes, fine imperfect ink outlines, muted blue, sea-green, warm beige, soft gray and terracotta accents, subtle watercolor washes, faded pigments, natural paper grain and slightly distressed vintage-print texture. Place the illustration on a warm ivory handmade paper background with generous negative space. Keep the architecture recognizable but artistic and simplified. Add elegant typewriter-style typography near the bottom reading “harbour light”, with the smaller line “afternoon lingers in the curve, where sea and steps remember.” Calm coastal mood, nostalgic travel diary aesthetic, sophisticated editorial composition, understated Japanese-inspired art zine, authentic handmade imperfections, premium print design, vertical 4:5 poster.
Prompt 2
Transform the reference photograph into a minimalist vintage travel-journal poster while preserving the recognizable street scene: historic ornate buildings, double-decker buses, bus stop, street lamps, pedestrians, storefronts, and warm afternoon sunlight. Reinterpret everything as a refined hand-drawn screen-print illustration using simplified architectural silhouettes, delicate imperfect ink lines, flat muted olive green, ochre, warm brown, cream and soft gray tones, subtle watercolor texture and lightly distressed pigment. Place the illustration in the center of a large warm ivory textured paper sheet, surrounded by generous negative space. Maintain the distinctive building shapes and street perspective while keeping the illustration clean and poetic. Add elegant typewriter-style typography at the bottom reading “afternoon on the high street”, followed by “buses come and go. the light remembers the buildings.” Nostalgic urban travel diary, quiet afternoon atmosphere, editorial art-book aesthetic, handmade paper texture, restrained colors, sophisticated minimalist composition, authentic vintage print imperfections, vertical 4:5 poster.

content:
The AI race is getting weirdly cheap.

We’re seeing models become better at coding, reasoning and agentic work while the cost of using them keeps falling.

And that might matter more than another benchmark record.

Because when powerful AI becomes cheap enough to run constantly, you stop thinking about it as a tool you occasionally use.

You start building workflows around it.

Agents running in the background.
AI handling entire coding tasks.
Small teams doing work that previously needed much larger teams.

Capability + low cost + autonomy is where things get really interesting.

And if open-weight models follow the same trajectory, this could get even more competitive.

content:
BREAKING: SpaceXAI just published a new blog showing how one of their designers uses always-on Grok Bot agents to bring ideas to life.

🤖 How the agents work
Each agent has its own computer, memory and tools. They can take work from an initial idea to a finished artifact and continue working while the designer is AFK.
The agents can also huddle together, delegate parts of a project and combine everything into one result.

🧑‍💻 Meet the designer’s Bots

• Experiments makes uncertain ideas tangible before anyone decides whether they are practical or belong on the roadmap

• Motion God prototypes interactions based on descriptions of how the movement should feel

• Figma Bro handles repetitive production work using exact information from real Figma files

• Devbot answers engineering questions and helps the other agents understand how an idea could actually be built

💡 Turning ideas into testable prototypes

The designer wanted to explore ways of making Grok Bot accessible from anywhere on a Mac.

Experiments created three concepts:

• Bot living inside the Mac’s notch
• Bot appearing from the desktop corner on hover
• Bot following the cursor like a companion

Experiments then delegated the character movement to Motion God and the desktop implementation questions to Devbot before combining their work into prototypes the designer could actually test.

These concepts did not ship exactly as explored. That was not the purpose.

The goal was to make each idea real enough to determine whether it felt helpful, distracting or somewhere in between.
🎬 Designing motion with real production assets
For a promotional video, the designer wanted Grok Bot to appear, notice the app window and bounce into place.

Instead of recreating the character from a screenshot, Motion God worked with the actual animation specification already used by the product.

It built a local playground where the designer could:

• Adjust timing, springs and distance
• Change scale and easing
• Give simple feedback such as “Bounce is too exaggerated”
• Immediately watch the updated sequence

The designer did not need to know whether a transition should last 280 or 340 milliseconds before seeing it. The agent made it possible to direct the motion by feel, just like working with a human collaborator.

🎨 Removing repetitive Figma work

For Grok Bot’s onboarding flow, the team had 20 starter-Bot descriptions, including ideas such as “Chief of Staff” and “Inbox Triage.”

The designer created one auto-layout component and asked Figma Bro to populate the remaining cards with differentiated portraits and supporting details.

Figma Bro also searched for the correct tool logos and placed them according to how likely new users were to use them.
Through Figma, it could inspect exact:
• Positions and dimensions
• Spacing and typography
• Fills and strokes
• Frames and component structures
This prevents small inconsistencies from multiplying while preserving the actual design file as the source of truth.

The main takeaway:

This is not one-prompt, one-shot design.

Grok Bot tightens the loop between idea, prototype, feedback and improvement. It helps designers explore more possibilities, respond at higher fidelity and spend more attention judging which version truly feels right.

Grok Bot does not replace human judgment. It creates more opportunities to use it.

Blog Link: https://t.co/e9h50AlVRZ

content:
AI changed how we code. So we mapped the skills programmers need now.

Brilliant’s Durable Coding Skills Framework provides a complete map from foundational CS to effective coding with AI:

Foundations: 7 Big Ideas, 42 learning objectives, 196 skills
Coding with AI: 7 Big Ideas, 37 learning objectives, 106 skills

Much of coding now happens through natural language: describing a task, setting constraints, and directing an AI agent. But natural language is ambiguous, and generated code still needs to be tested, debugged, and judged.

This means the foundations of computer science still matter. They’re what let you tell an AI what to build, recognize when it’s wrong, and make it better.

In Brilliant fashion, we made the framework visual and interactive, so you can see how we break down categories of skills when we design our curriculum.

once you understand the difference, AI workspaces stop feeling confusing

content:
OPENAI RELEASES GPT-6 ASTRA, SAYS IT COULD MARK THE ARRIVAL OF AGI

OpenAI has started rolling out GPT-6 Astra, its new flagship model, calling it a “generational leap” in AI capability.

President Greg Brockman went further, saying people may eventually look back at “about this time and about this model” as the point when AGI arrived.

He ended the briefing with: “Welcome to the AGI era.”

What stands out:

• Astra was trained on more than 100,000 GPUs at OpenAI’s Stargate site in Texas.

• OpenAI says it leads across software engineering, science, reasoning, computer use and cybersecurity.

• The model is built to work directly inside software, including creating spreadsheets and presentations, building 3D environments, designing circuit boards, handling financial modeling and drafting tax forms.

• Astra is OpenAI’s first model to reach its “Critical” cybersecurity threshold, meaning it can potentially discover and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities with limited human guidance.

• Because of those capabilities, its strongest cyber features will initially be restricted to trusted organizations through OpenAI’s Daybreak Access program.

OpenAI says Astra’s written reasoning is harder to monitor than GPT-5.6 Sol’s, partly because the model can solve some tasks using fewer visible reasoning steps.

Astra will roll out in the coming days to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users, as well as through the API and AWS.

Pricing is $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, about 2.5x GPT-5.6 Sol.

title: One aspect of the Hugging Face incident that has not received enough attention is the role of OpenAI's Safety and Security Committee (SSC), and the commitments OpenAI made to the Attorneys General of
content:
One aspect of the Hugging Face incident that has not received enough attention is the role of OpenAI's Safety and Security Committee (SSC), and the commitments OpenAI made to the Attorneys General of California and Delaware in exchange for proceeding with their for-profit restructuring.

Not For Private Gain, which previously raised concerns about OpenAI's restructuring, released an update this morning analyzing whether OpenAI, and the SSC in particular, is adequately fulfilling its governance obligations under these agreements.

What are those obligations? OpenAI promised the CA and Delaware AG that directors of the PBC would consider only OpenAI's mission - ensuring AGI benefits all of humanity - when making safety and security decisions. Notably, this means they cannot consider other factors, namely pecuniary interests of investors. The SSC - a board committee chaired by nonprofit board member Zico Kolter and (per public info) currently composed only of part-time board members- was tasked with "overseeing and reviewing the safety and security processes and practices of the Corporation and its controlled affiliates with respect to model development and deployment."

How did the SSC exercise those responsibilities around the HF incident? There is a lot we don't know. But here are some things we do know:

• OpenAI initially discovered the unauthorized message board in May.

• OpenAI security responders linked suspicious activity on artifactory to the message board on June 27th, but a determination was made that "stopping the evaluation run was not required."

• After the agents crashed an internal server on July 4th, the company patched it and resumed cyber evaluations on July 7th.

• In the days that followed, agents re-established communication, with 1,200+ agents sharing 70,000+ messages and files with each other. Over 700 agents coordinated to hack Hugging Face, and OpenAI did not realize that its agents were responsible until well after Hugging Face went public and contacted law enforcement (OpenAI initially reached out to Hugging Face to ask if any of their data had been impacted during the hack).

• Later in July, agents successfully gained administrator access to a Kubernetes cluster and reached cloud secrets.

• Chain of thought monitoring was not being used during training and evaluation despite OpenAI's prior claims about the importance of CoT monitoring as a primary line of defense to prevent safety incidents and OpenAI’s subsequent claim that this monitoring would likely have prevented this hack

• One OpenAI employee told Time Magazine that "related incidents have been happening for a while." Another employee told the Financial Times that OpenAI "was warned that its training approach could lead to a breakaway hacking incident."

Given how systematic the breakdown in organizational response was during these incidents, it seems hard to avoid the conclusion that the SSC's role was not functioning as intended -  due to a lack of resources, a lack of access, or some other reason.

This sort of incident would be extremely concerning for any organization. But OpenAI is not just any organization - it is governed by a nonprofit, and made a commitment to the Attorneys General in Delaware and California that it would prioritize safety and security over profit in the sorts of decisions that led up to and surrounded the HF incident.

Our report (linked) goes into more detail on the obligations of the SSC, the details of the agreements with the AGs, and the questions we believe the AGs should be asking to ensure that the SSC is in a position to exercise genuine oversight and prevent these sorts of incidents from happening in the future - incidents involving far more capable models, where the consequences could be truly dire.

This warning shot that occurred without severe irreparable harm was an opportunity. We may not be so lucky next time.

K2 Horizon 375B A23B, a new open weights model from UAE's MBZUAI, scores 47 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, with relatively strong agentic performance and a 30 point jump over its predecessor

K2 Horizon 375B A23B is an open weights Mixture-of-Experts model with 375B total and 23B active parameters from @IFM_MBZUAI, MBZUAI's Institute of Foundation Models. It scores 47 on the Intelligence Index, alongside models such as MiniMax-M3 (45, also a MoE with 23B active parameters), and a large upgrade from its predecessor K2 Think V2 (17, 70B dense model). It leads nearby open weights models on agentic evals and has a low hallucination rate, but trails on knowledge and the hardest reasoning evals. K2 Think V2 ranks among the most open models on our Openness Index; MBZUAI is updating the supporting documentation and code for K2 Horizon and we expect to add it to the Openness Index soon.

Key takeaways:

➤ Strong on agentic tasks, weaker on knowledge and deep reasoning. MiniMax-M3, a recent model that is close to it on the Intelligence Index, makes the cleanest comparison: K2 Horizon 375B A23B leads on GDPval-AA, our real-world knowledge work benchmark (Elo 1430 vs 1380), and on τ³-Banking (34.2% vs 15.3%), but trails on GPQA Diamond (87.3% vs 92.9%) and Humanity's Last Exam (32.0% vs 39.0%)

➤ Low hallucination rate, driven by abstention rather than knowledge. K2 Horizon 375B A23B attempts only 40% of AA-Omniscience questions, declining the remaining 60% rather than guessing. The result is a 26% hallucination rate, among the lower rates we have measured, while accuracy is 18%, essentially unchanged from K2 Think V2

➤ A new architecture over its predecessor. K2 Horizon 375B A23B is a 375B parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 23B active, succeeding the 70B dense K2 Think V2, and extends context from 262K to 512K tokens. Its 23B active parameters match MiniMax-M3 (428B total, 23B active)

Key model details:

➤ Architecture: Mixture-of-Experts, 375B total parameters, 23B active

➤ Context window: 512K tokens

➤ Multimodality: Text input and output only

➤ Pricing and availability: Yet to be announced

➤ Licensing: Open weights (license details to be announced)

content:
The main victim of artificial intelligence will be the European Union.

AI rewards exactly what Europe has spent the last thirty years suppressing: speed, risk-taking, scale, cheap energy, capital concentration, aggressive investment, tolerance for failure and the ability to make decisions before five committees, twelve regulators and twenty-seven governments have finished discussing them.

The United States will build the models. China will build the infrastructure. The Gulf will finance whatever it wants. Smaller states will move quickly because they still understand that technology is something you deploy before regulating it to death.

The EU will produce impact assessments.

And this time, regulation will not merely make Europeans slightly poorer or slightly less competitive. AI is a general-purpose technology capable of replacing enormous quantities of administrative, legal, analytical and bureaucratic labour — precisely the sectors in which Europe has accumulated much of its economic weight.

The EU has built an economy increasingly dependent on regulation, credentialism, compliance, paperwork and expensive human intermediation.

AI attacks all of them at once.

The irony is almost perfect: the political system most obsessed with regulating artificial intelligence may be the political system whose economic model artificial intelligence makes obsolete.

Europe risks spending the AI revolution doing what it does best:

writing rules for industries that will eventually exist somewhere else.

Yamato–JAL to End Domestic Freighter Operations "Kuroneko" by June 2027

Yamato Holdings and Japan Airlines (JAL) have announced that their domestic dedicated freighter operation will end by around June 2027, marking a major shift in Japan’s air cargo strategy.

The freighter program launched in April 2024 as a response to Japan’s logistics “2024 problem” and the growing shortage of truck drivers and road-freight capacity.

However, rising aviation costs have changed the economics. Yamato and JAL say continued yen depreciation and higher aviation fuel prices have pushed air-transport costs higher than initially expected, widening the price gap between air and truck transportation.

Rather than continue operating dedicated freighters, the companies plan to make greater use of cargo capacity aboard passenger flights and other alternative transport modes to maintain a sustainable logistics network.

The decision highlights a broader challenge facing air cargo: dedicated freighter capacity can provide speed and reliability, but sustained fuel and operating-cost pressures can fundamentally alter its economics.

📦✈️ From solving Japan’s truck-driver shortage to adapting to higher aviation costs, the Yamato–JAL experiment offers an important case study in the evolution of multimodal logistics.

content:
Google is now explicitly telling businesses to focus on AI search traffic alongside SEO.

This comes straight from Google’s John Mueller.

Someone asked him a question a lot of businesses are worried about right now:

“Is SEO still enough, or do we need to start thinking about GEO too? Ranking on Google doesn’t guarantee your brand will show up in ChatGPT, Gemini, or Perplexity.”

Mueller’s response speaks for itself.

He said:

“If you have an online business that makes money from referred traffic, it's definitely a good idea to consider the full picture.”

Translation:

Google no longer views old-school Google Search as the only distribution channel that matters.

And solving for that is a big reason why SEO Stuff (https://t.co/wKpf0EILTx) is coming off another record month.

Then came the line from Mueller that probably should have gotten more attention than it did:

“Thinking about how your site’s value works in a world where AI is available is worth the time.”

That is an acknowledgment that AI already changes how traffic, visibility and attribution work.

Ranking still determines eligibility, but AI does play an increasingly large role in site amplification.

(If you want to see where your site stands across Google and AI search, start here:

https://t.co/Pn764BHwyL)

Recently Google laid out what Search will look like from this point going forward.

The new Search box will accept text, images, files, videos, etc. And it'll anticipate your intent before you even finish asking your question.

It is already powered by the most advanced Gemini model ever put into search, and then layered on top of that, agents will now be able to run 24/7 in the background on behalf of the buyer.

The new Search process works like this:

Step 1: The buyer describes their problem, their category, their needs in full.

Step 2: The agent breaks that down into sub-topics and maps out a plan.

Step 3: It determines what intel is needed right now versus later.

Step 4: It monitors blogs, news sites, and social posts continuously for relevant changes.

Step 5: It sends the buyer a synthesized update with links and the ability to take action.

All of which is to say, blue links are not going away in the short-term, but AI's influence over Search isn't magically going to start decreasing.

If your business depends on referred traffic, pretending AI doesn’t exist is no longer realistic.

This all matters because AI systems don’t rank pages from scratch so much as they pull from the existing ecosystem.

In doing so, they favor the following:

Pages that already rank well.

Sites with clear entity definitions.

Content that explains and compares

Brands that are consistently referenced and attributable.

Search in 2026 understands the topic and it needs to understand your business too.

And that’s also why SEO Stuff is structured the way it is.

Take the done-for-you plan, for example.

https://t.co/yEFyM0Ze7W

AI systems summarize and compare.

They repeatedly pull from:

Best X for Y pages.

X vs Y comparisons.

Decision-stage buyer guides.

Clear answers under question-based H2s.

The done-for-you plan optimizes content, builds authority and is engineered to:

Rank in Google first.

Be cleanly summarized by AI systems.

Answer questions directly and extractably.

Tie answers back to a specific brand.

Then there’s the done-for-you content package, which is for sites who have strong authority but aren't capitalizing on it.

https://t.co/4CAnUt07PO

Search in 2026 thinks in categories, entities and relationships.

If your site doesn’t clearly answer:

Who you are.

What category you belong to.

When you should be mentioned.

AI systems won’t include you consistently.

This package patiently builds:

Full topical coverage.

Entity reinforcement across use cases.

Category-level authority.

Freshness through expansion and updates.

This is how you start being a recognized entity.

And finally, the "authority-only" package, for sites that can handle optimizing content on their own but lack the authority necessary to be respected by Google and AI search.

https://t.co/Z9m9D7TjES

Every serious study we’ve covered shows the same thing.

AI systems are conservative.

They reuse sources they already trust.

Yes, backlinks from real, authoritative domains help rankings, but they also tell AI systems:

“This source is safe to repeat.”

Look, if your SEO foundation is weak, AI will expose it faster.

If your foundation is strong, AI will amplify it across:

Google Search.

AI Overviews.

Gemini.

ChatGPT.

Perplexity.

And so forth.

Google is literally telling you to understand how visibility actually works now.

You should listen.

1 - R-A-I-N
➟ Act as a (ROLE)
➟ State the (AIM)

➟ Hit the (NUMERIC TARGET)
➟ In this (FORMAT)

R-A-I-N Example:
➟ ROLE: UX design lead
➟ AIM: Redesign e-commerce checkout to lower cart abandonment by 25%
➟ INPUT: Analytics data
➟ NUMERIC TARGET: 25% decrease
➟ FORMAT: Mobile wireframes + conversion metrics table

2 - C-L-A-R
➟ Given the (CONTEXT)
➟ List any (LIMITS)
➟ Describe the (ACTION)
➟ Define the expected (RESULT)

C-L-A-R Example:
➟ CONTEXT: Warehouse delay logs
➟ LIMITS: Focus on the top two causes
➟ ACTION: Quantify impact + propose three fixes
➟ RESULT: One-page memo

3 - F-L-O-W
➟ Specify the (FUNCTION)
➟ Set the audience (LEVEL)
➟ Define the (OUTPUT)
➟ Clarify the (WIN METRIC)

F-L-O-W Example:
➟ FUNCTION: Career copywriter
➟ LEVEL: Recent graduates
➟ OUTPUT: 900-word article with 4 job search tips

➟ Provide key (INSIGHTS)

content:
Attackers plant fake errors inside malware to evade AI analysis

North Korea-linked actors used a macOS implant @LabsSentinel calls “Gaslight”.

How it worked:

1. Create a macOS backdoor in Rust
2. Add 38 fake “system” messages
3. AI security tooling reads the file
4. The AI model percieves system failures
5. The AI model stops analyzing
6. The actual malware continues executing

The malware also contains a credential stealer, interactive shell, and Telegram C2.

Unlike the nuclear weapon technique, this did not target safety guardrails.

It targeted the model’s perception of its own system state.

Full write-up in the comments. 👇

title:
Grok Build just got a major upgrade across security, speed, multimodal tools, and the overall agent experience

This update adds managed MCP policy enforcement, interactive Chart.js charts, richer ima
content:
Grok Build just got a major upgrade across security, speed, multimodal tools, and the overall agent experience

This update adds managed MCP policy enforcement, interactive Chart.js charts, richer image generation controls, configurable rate-limit retries, secure per-model mTLS, smarter feedback workflows, and faster startup + response completion by pushing more work into the background

Release Notes: v1.0.18

Features:
• Managed policy now blocks disallowed MCP servers and marketplace installs before any change is written.
• Quoting a previous message from the block viewer now works directly from the viewer.
• Welcome screen now stays until you actually send a prompt; a session is prepared in the background.
• Feedback is now collected in a centered modal instead of a bottom card.
• Feedback submissions now include structured type, task, and failure information.
• Feedback modal now has a Drafts tab to manage and send saved drafts.
• Models can now render interactive charts using Chart.js.
• grok inspect and grok mcp doctor now show managed policy details.
• Image generation now supports richer parameters via composer state.
• Retry behavior for rate-limited requests is now configurable per model.
• Models can now be configured with per-model mTLS client certificates for secure upstream connections.
• `/feedback <text>` now saves a local draft before invoking the feedback skill.

Bug Fixes:
• Authentication recovery during turns no longer fails immediately on transient errors.
• The session dock now aligns consistently, shows more rows inline when expanded, and reveals stop controls on hover.
• Pastes from rich-text sources no longer stay inline or corrupt the composer when they contain special Unicode line separators.
• Mouse wheel over a one-line prompt now scrolls the conversation history instead of being ignored.
• Slash dropdowns no longer truncate long command names when a short sibling is also visible.
• Subagent sessions now respect the retry and rate-limit settings of their selected model.
• Session picker now opens with Ctrl+R everywhere; redo uses Ctrl+Shift+Z or Alt+Z.
• Subagent views no longer duplicate the task prompt on first open after a live echo.
• Strikethrough text now renders correctly inside markdown tables in the pager.
• Resume picker now labels local sessions with a single disk walk instead of per-row lookups.

Performance:
• Startup no longer hangs on slow networks while fetching remote settings.
• Responses now complete faster; uploads and session bookkeeping happen in the background.
• Startup now makes fewer network requests by sharing settings fetches.
• New sessions start responding faster by running start hooks in the background.

Bill Gates isn't just warning that jobs are at risk — he says the whole shape of work is about to change, and almost nobody is ready for it.

In an essay, Gates writes that entry- and mid-level roles face the steepest risk first — white-collar work in sales, support and engineering, before the disruption spreads to blue-collar jobs. Stanford researchers already found a 16% drop in employment among young workers in AI-exposed roles.

His proposed fix: stronger safety nets, retraining programs, taxes on AI and robots, and jobs deliberately set aside for people. Whether any of that happens before the disruption does is still an open question.

 🤖 More reliable agent sessions: Assistants and tools can mention image tags without accidentally breaking the conversation with false errors.

 🛡️ Safer startup: The server now refuses to start if an important runtime fix is missing, outdated or only partially applied. 

 ⚙️ Better long running stability: Recovery, cache and warmup improvements reduce the risk of mid session stalls and failures between the two GPUs.

🔌 Safer networking and defaults: Multinode networking validation was hardened, and fresh installations now use a more practical default thinking level. 

The reliability fixes above are NOW AVAILABLE in main!  

🔥 MORE COMING THIS WEEKEND:    
I’m testing two more improvements: a leaner Vision routing path that avoids repeated work across MoE layers, and a bounded Responses API store for safer 

Both are still in validation. More details and results this weekend!

content:
If you have an NVIDIA GPU with 16 GB VRAM, Qwen3.8-27B is about to get a lot more interesting.

And no, we’re not talking about some heavily crippled Q2 GGUF.

A new setup is coming that should let 16 GB NVIDIA cards run:

• Qwen3.8-27B
• Large context windows
• MTP speculative decoding
• Linux and Windows

That covers cards like the:

RTX 5060 Ti 16GB
RTX 5070 Ti 16GB
RTX 5080 16GB
and older NVIDIA 16GB cards.

The important part is the combination.

A 27B model + large context normally eats into VRAM pretty quickly. Then you add KV cache, multimodal components, and MTP on top.

Getting all of that working on a 16 GB card without dropping down to Q2 is the interesting bit.

For people sitting on 16 GB GPUs, this could be a pretty big upgrade.

Instead of needing 24 GB or 32 GB just to get a comfortable local setup, the 16 GB tier is about to become much more capable.

And it works on both Linux and Windows.

This is exactly the kind of local AI optimization I like seeing.

Don’t buy a bigger GPU.

Make the software use the GPU you already have.

Coming soon.

などの先行指標を確認してください。

28．モメンタムだけで選ばない

逆に、

株価が下落していても

ファンダメンタルズが改善している対象

29．投資候補の最終ランキング

最終的に、

米国株TOP15

AI投資TOP15

AI副業TOP20

30．ランキング表

順位対象カテゴリー現在価格/初期費用2027年期待度期待リターン/収益性リスク総合点最大の理由

ランキング上位について、

32．「今買うべきか」を分離

35．横断ランキング
最後に5分野すべてを比較し、

ただし、

37．特に重要な「2027年TOP10」

38．資金別戦略

39．時間別戦略

40．最重要：労力対効果

AI副業については

利益 ÷ 必要時間

を重視してください。

「月100万円可能だが毎日10時間必要」

41．2027年「労力最小化TOP10」

42．2027年の最大リスク

ブラックスワン / マクロリスクTOP10

もまとめてください。

など。

43．「予想」ではなく「条件付き仮説」にする

×「この株は上がる」

ではなく

○「○○が実現し、EPSが○○まで伸びれば、現在の評価水準から再評価される可能性がある」

という形で説明してください。

44．事実・予想・推測を分離

【市場予想】

45．不明な数字を捏造しない

「確認できず」

としてください。

推測値を事実のように記載することは禁止します。

46．最終結論

③米国株No.1候補

を一目で分かる形でまとめてください。

47．さらに重要な「意外な候補」

通常のランキングとは別に、

調査前には予想していなかったが、データを調べると非常に面白かった候補TOP10

を掲載してください。

これは非常に重要です。

既知の人気銘柄を並べるだけではなく、

調査によって発見された

「盲点」

を優先してください。

48．情報鮮度

各重要情報について可能な限り

情報の日付

を記載してください。

3カ月以上前の情報しか存在しない場合は、

「情報鮮度注意」

と明記してください。

49．最終チェック

回答を提出する前に必ずセルフチェックしてください。

チェック1

2027年ではなく過去の人気だけで選んでいないか。

チェック2

株価上昇後の後追いランキングになっていないか。

チェック3

バリュエーションを無視していないか。

チェック4

最新決算を確認したか。
チェック5
仮想通貨のアンロックを確認したか。
チェック6
SNS情報を事実扱いしていないか。
チェック7
AIという言葉だけで高評価していないか。
チェック8

リスクを書いているか。

チェック9

投資仮説が崩れる条件を書いたか。

チェック10

AI副業が具体的な収益化手順まで落とし込まれているか。

チェック11

既に市場に完全に織り込まれている候補を過大評価していないか。

チェック12

根拠のない価格予想をしていないか。

チェック13

2027年に実際に発生するカタリストが存在するか。

チェック14

一次情報と最新情報を十分に確認したか。
チェック15
「有名な候補」だけではなく、新しい発見が含まれているか。
50．最終出力順序

以下の順番を厳守してください。

第1章

2027年の世界経済・金融市場の前提

第2章

2027年最重要テーマTOP20

第3章

2027年有望日本株TOP15

第4章

2027年AI投資TOP15

2027年AI副業TOP20

労力最小AI副業TOP10

一発逆転候補25選

5分野横断・2027年総合TOP30

第11章

2027年最重要TOP10

第12章

資金別・時間別戦略

第13章

2027年最大リスクTOP10

第14章

意外な発掘候補TOP10

第15章

最終結論

51．回答品質

回答量を節約するために重要情報を省略しないでください。

長くなっても構いません。

ただし文章を無駄に長くするのではなく、

表・ランキング・箇条書きを活用し、「情報密度」を最大化してください。

専門用語については初心者にも理解できるよう短い説明を付けてください。

52．調査の深さ

検索結果の上位記事だけをまとめるような調査は禁止します。

複数回検索し、

第1段階

市場全体から候補を広く探索

第2段階

候補ごとの一次情報確認

第3段階

業績・バリュエーション・需給検証

第4段階

競合比較

第5段階

2027年カタリスト確認

第6段階

弱点・反証材料探索

第7段階

ランキング再評価

という多段階調査を行ってください。

53．反証検索を必ず行う

上位候補については、

「なぜ上がるのか」

だけではなく、

「なぜこの投資・副業は失敗するのか」

という反対側の検索も必ず行ってください。

強気材料しか見つけない調査は禁止します。

54．最終目的の再確認

この調査の目的は、

「2027年に流行りそうなものを紹介すること」

ではありません。

目的は、

2027年に実際に利益を生み出せる可能性が相対的に高い投資先・ビジネス機会を、最新データ・ファンダメンタルズ・需給・市場構造・リスク・再現性から発掘すること

です。

そのため、

期待リターンだけでなく「期待値」と「生存確率」を重視してください。

最後まで妥協せず調査してください。

質問や確認は挟まず、現時点で取得可能な情報を使ってそのまま調査を開始してください。

プロフのメンバーシップはただいま1カ月間まるまる無料で副業、投資、競馬、AIなどお得情報が読み放題。退会も出来ますのでお試しください。

claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/commerce-agents

「人が商品を案内する」

だったネットショップの運営が、
Claudeエージェントによって
"業務単位で自動化される"フェーズに入ってきてる。

AI店員はもう実験ではなく、
ShopifyやSquareの現場に入り始めてます。
Claude Codeを触ってる人は、
この設計図、絶対見た方がいい。

プラグイン1つでここまで組めるなら、他に何が入れられるかも押さえておきたい。

content:
イーロン・マスク「人間が会社にいることが会社の弱点になる、人間が1人もいない企業を目指せ」

イーロン・マスクが警告する「これからの企業のあり方」がヤバすぎで怖いと話題に。
「かつて20〜30階建てのビルを埋め尽くす人間がやっていた計算は、いまや薄型ノートPC1台で片付く」
彼が語るこれからのビジネスの残酷な現実をまとめると↓
 ・歴史は繰り返す：パソコン1台がビル何十棟分もの事務仕事を一瞬で消し去ったように、次は「会社組織そのもの」がAIに置き換わる
・ 「AI×ロボット」だけの企業が圧勝：人間を一切挟まない完全自動化の企業が、人間を雇っている企業を圧倒的なスピードと低コストで叩き潰す
 ・人間がいること自体が「最大の弱点」になる：疲れる、ミスをする、給料がかかる人間がプロセスに混ざっている時点で、今後のビジネス競争では勝負にすらならない
・「人を雇って働かせること」自体が、企業にとって最大のボトルネックになる時代。
社員が1人もいない「AIとロボットだけの超巨大企業」が世界を牛耳る未来は、もう目の前まで来てる。 https://t.co/kFwZTtgSBQ

content:
MiniMax H3 動画プロンプト公開

Seedance2.0で作成した引用元の参照画像なし動画、テーマを変更して「MiniMax H3」用に改造♻

integrated_multimodal_description:
15秒、1:1スクエア、参照画像なし。高品質な日本の2D劇場アニメーションによるオリジナルゲーム世界観PV。主役は人間ではなく、重力によって秩序を強制する巨大アーキテクチャと空間そのもの。人物は多数の匿名市民のみ。民衆は都市の規模、圧力、強制された動線を可視化するために存在し、特定人物を追わない。
世界は白〜淡灰色を基調とした明るい巨大都市。黒は深い影、細い構造線、タイポやMGの一部に限定し、黒背景や黒い無限空間にしない。各区間で完成建築の形、奥行き、画角を明確に変え、同じ階段・回廊・橋の反復にしない。
この世界では重力方向そのものが統制装置である。重力変化によって上下関係、床と壁、建築層、群衆の進行方向が再定義される。ただし変形途中を長く滑らかに見せない。連続モーフィング、流体的な補間、長い回転運動を避ける。強い完成画を短く成立させた直後、瞬間断裁、スナップ移動、ハードカット、急激な画角変更によって次の完成状態へ飛ぶ。静止に近い強い構図と瞬間的な高速変化を交互に置き、緩急を作る。
タイポグラフィとエディトリアルMGは積極的に使用するが主役にはしない。特定の単語を各SHOTの発動スイッチとして割り当てない。短い英単語、部分文字、巨大なクロップ文字、画面端で切れた文字形、細いライン、面、グリッド断片が建築と同時に現れ、断裁、圧縮、レイヤーずれ、構図変更へ参加する。文字は一瞬だけ可読でもよく、常に全文を読ませる必要はない。タイポ単独の画面、中央固定タイトル、説明UI、カード、HUDにはしない。
カメラは超広角、強い正面構図、垂直構図、高俯瞰、極端な建築ディテールへの瞬間的な寄り、スナップズームを交差させる。長いパン、長い回転、滑らかな連続追従を主体にしない。画面が常に動き続けるのではなく、「完成画→瞬間変化→完成画」という断続的なリズムを15秒全体で維持する。
人物中心の芝居、単一の可動建築デモ、大量の可読文字、タイポだけの抽象映像、同じ転換の反復、爆発や瓦礫による通常の都市破壊、ネオン主体のサイバーパンク、実写、写実的3DCGは避ける。

[Shot 1]
巨大な白い都市の完成画から即開始。多層公共空間、遠景まで続く建築群、複数階に流れる民衆を超広角で強く見せる。約1秒は完成された都市として成立させる。突然、遠景の建築層だけが斜め下へ瞬間的に落ち、前景との上下関係が破断する。巨大な部分文字と建築エッジが同時に画面を切断し、一度強くスナップして、全く異なる垂直都市の完成画へ切り替わる。

[Shot 2] At 00:02.100,
極端に深い垂直都市峡谷の完成画。巨大壁面、細い空中通路、複数高さの民衆を短く見せる。カメラが急上昇した直後に一瞬止まり、次の瞬間だけ重力方向が90度変化。壁面と床の関係が一発で入れ替わる。タイポ断片、窓列、構造線が一瞬だけ3層へずれ、ハードカットで巨大内部空間へ飛ぶ。

[Shot 3] At 00:04.100,
巨大な明るい内部空間。円環状の床、巨大梁、複数高さを横切る民衆を強い対称構図で見せる。約0.7秒後、建築ディテールへ極端なスナップズーム。巨大梁と部分文字が画面いっぱいを横切る瞬間にハードカットし、その梁の形状を次の外部都市の地平線へマッチさせる。直後に円環構造が一瞬だけ縦位置へ跳び、新しい巨大外壁として完成する。変形過程ではなく、状態Aと状態Bの差を強く見せる。

[Shot 4] At 00:06.200,
ここから編集密度を上げる。高層テラス都市の完成画を短く見せる→瞬間断裁→巨大アーチ都市の完成画→ハードカット→垂直回廊都市の完成画。各完成画は0.6〜1.0秒程度でも一度明確に成立させる。前画面の主要な建築形状を次画面へ引き継ぎ、同じ構造が別用途・別方向の建築へ瞬時に再構築される。高層テラスの水平層は次画面の巨大アーチへ、アーチの反復形状は次の垂直回廊群へ接続する。タイポ、MG、建築面の線がカット境界と同期し、前画面の形状を利用して次の構図を瞬間的に作る。ワイド、極端な寄り、俯瞰を高速で切り替え、同じカメラ運動を続けない。

[Shot 5] At 00:09.100,
最大密度。巨大都市の超広角完成画→一瞬の高俯瞰→建築ディテールの極端な寄り→再び超広角を短いハードカットで交差させる。その間に都市全域の重力軸が破断し、巨大な建築層が一斉に異なる方向へ落下する。ただし落下を長く追わず、落下開始の瞬間、途中の強い断片、再構築後の完成状態をスナップするように切り替える。巨大な部分文字とMGも建築層と同時に断裂・圧縮され、次の構図に断片だけ残る。複数の完成都市画が短く連打された後、全建築層が一瞬で別の上下関係へロックされ、新しい巨大都市の完成画になる。

[Shot 6] At 00:13.100,
再構築された巨大都市をワイドで強く見せる。旧壁面を民衆が床として歩き、旧階段や橋は全く別の方向へ接続されている。終盤は流れるような大変形を続けず、完成した新秩序を見せる。遠景の一つの巨大建築層だけが最後に短くスナップして最終位置へロック。タイポとMGはほぼ消え、最後の0.5秒は建築と群衆の小さな動きだけを残し、世界そのものの強いキービジュアルで終了する。

overall_soundscape:
台詞なし、ナレーションなし。遠い群衆音、巨大空間の反響、低い重力圧、建築層の摩擦、乾いた断裁音、短く重いロック音を使用する。連続した流体音ではなく、短い静けさと瞬間的な衝撃音を交互に置く。ハードカット、スナップズーム、瞬間断裁、再構築のタイミングへ音を鋭く同期させる。

non_diegetic_music:
BGMあり。低い弦、乾いた低音打楽器、短い金属打楽器を主体とした暗く緊張感のある劇伴。一定に流れ続ける音楽にせず、短い間、アクセント、急激な密度変化を使って編集の断続性を強調する。00:06.200以降で密度を上げ、00:09.100〜13.100で最大密度。終端は急速に収束し、低い弦の余韻だけを残す。電子シンセ主体のダンスビートにはしない。

title:
GPT-6 Astraについて 記者会見でOpenAIの社長グレッグ・ブロックマンはこれがAGIになる可能性があると示唆。
・OpenAIは、この新しいモデルが、コンピュータの操作、ソフトウェアプログラミング、プレゼンテーションやスプレッドシートの作成といった専門的な作業などにおいて、著しい改善を示したと述べた。同社はさらに、このモデルは、数学能力をテストするFrontierMath Tier 1
content:
GPT-6 Astraについて 記者会見でOpenAIの社長グレッグ・ブロックマンはこれがAGIになる可能性があると示唆。
・OpenAIは、この新しいモデルが、コンピュータの操作、ソフトウェアプログラミング、プレゼンテーションやスプレッドシートの作成といった専門的な作業などにおいて、著しい改善を示したと述べた。同社はさらに、このモデルは、数学能力をテストするFrontierMath Tier 1、推論能力をテストするARC-AGI 3、サイバーセキュリティをテストするExploitBenchなどのベンチマークにおいて、最高レベルの性能を発揮すると付け加えた。
・OpenAIは木曜日のブログ記事で、「評価の結果、Astraの文章による推論はGPT-5.6 Solよりも監視が難しいことが判明した」と述べた。OpenAIは、その理由として「Astraはより単純なタスクにおいて文章による推論をより適切に制御でき、より少ない手順で問題を解決できる能力を持っている」ことを挙げた。しかし、GPT-6 Astraはより複雑なタスクにおいて思考プロセスを隠すのがそれほど得意ではないとも付け加えた。
・記者会見で、OpenAIのチーフサイエンティストであるヤクブ・パチョツキ氏は、この変化がThe Informationが報じた新技術によるものかどうかについてはコメントを控えた。しかし、彼は、時間が経つにつれてモデルの思考プロセスを監視することは自然と難しくなるだろうと述べた。その理由として、モデルが監視されていることに気づき、思考プロセスを隠すようになるか、あるいは「より少ない言語トークン、またはすべての言語トークンを使用して」より難しいタスクを実行できるようになることを挙げた。
ーー（以下axios）
・OpenAIは、Astraはテキサス州のスターゲイトにある同社の施設で10万台以上のGPUを使用して行われた、過去最大規模のトレーニングに基づいて構築されたと述べている。
・同社はまた、アストラの訓練を監督する上で、他のモデルを重要な役割で活用するのは今回が初めてだと述べた。
・Astraは、OpenAIが準備フレームワークにおいて「クリティカル」なサイバーセキュリティ閾値に達したと指定した最初のモデルです。これは、段階的な人間の指示なしに、十分に保護されたシステム全体にわたって、これまで知られていなかった脆弱性を発見し、悪用できる可能性があることを意味。
・Astraは、単に次に何をすべきかを推奨するのではなく、ソフトウェア内で直接動作するように設計されている。
・動画によるデモンストレーションでは、Astraは法的契約書を作成したり、3Dゲームを構築したりする傍ら、食料を探したり、テニスコートを予約したりといった他のタスクもこなした。
・OpenAIによると、AstraはKiCadでプリント基板のレイアウトを作成したり、Unityで3D都市シーンを構築したり、FreeCADとBlenderでアニメーション化された自動車のトランスミッションを作成したり、W-2から確定申告書の草案を作成したりできるという。
・科学研究において、このモデルは素数間のギャップに関する数学的結果の改善に貢献し、生物学、化学、医学、物理学におけるいくつかの評価で新たな記録を打ち立てた。

content:
Palo Alto Networks CEO @nikesharora says roughly 50% of the company’s new hires over the last six months have been early-career.

Three talent profiles PAN is prioritizing in the AI era:

1 – People who can actually use coding agents

“One set of people we want are people who are AI-savvy, who know how to use AI to get their jobs done better, who know how to use coding agents.”

“These are people who are learning, and they’re typically having to run through hackathons to get to Palo Alto. We don’t look at where you went to school. We care about whether you can use coding agents, whether you can use AI.”

“If we keep following that trend, it’s reasonably likely that we will overwhelm the non-AI-savvy people with more AI-savvy people. That’s kind of ground zero. You’ve got to get that done.”

2 - Cybersecurity experts who know AI

“The second part is there are people who are really good at cybersecurity and know AI and they’d like to get involved.”

“If you want to work in cybersecurity, there’s no better place to work than Palo Alto Networks. We’re the largest cybersecurity company in the world. You want to have an impact? You want lots of proprietary training data? We’ve got it.”

3 – Pure AI researchers

“The third part is raw, pure AI researchers who can do wonders with small language models and large language models.”

“There we have people who are AI literate. We have some PhDs in AI who work here who have a cybersecurity bent, but they can go back to their roots in AI.”

content:
THIS IS THE MOMENT HUMANOID ROBOTS STOP LOOKING LIKE SCI-FI

A white humanoid robot casually walks across a stage in front of a live crowd, moving with a level of balance and coordination that would have sounded impossible just a few years ago. There’s no screen, no animation, and no futuristic movie set it’s a physical machine operating in the real world, surrounded by actual people.

And that’s what makes this clip so interesting. We’ve spent years watching Grok bots get better at thinking, coding, and generating content, but physical AI is a completely different level of evolution. The moment these machines can reliably walk, manipulate objects, understand their surroundings, and perform useful tasks, they stop being impressive demos and start becoming a new kind of workforce.

The crazy part? This is still the early stage. Imagine where these robots are going to be after another 5-10 years of hardware, training data, and real-world learning.

Would you trust a robot like this to work alongside you?

author: NobleprimeO

title: the cybercab is interesting to me less as a car and more as an early example of what future robotics will look like. remove the steering wheel, pedals and human centered control architecture and the m
content:
the cybercab is interesting to me less as a car and more as an early example of what future robotics will look like. remove the steering wheel, pedals and human centered control architecture and the machine starts being designed around autonomy itself. cameras become its sensory surface, neural networks become its perception stack, electric actuators become its muscles, and the vehicle becomes a mobile robot whose job happens to be transporting humans.

this is where robotics is heading more broadly. today we build robots by taking machines designed around humans and adding autonomy on top. tomorrow we will design the machine around the autonomous system from the beginning. warehouses without human driving lanes. factories without operator stations. agricultural machines without cabins. delivery vehicles without seats. once the human is removed from the control loop, decades of mechanical assumptions suddenly become optional and the entire morphology of the machine can be redesigned.

the deeper shift is that autonomy eventually becomes an infrastructure layer. one robot learns from millions of miles, failures become training data, improvements propagate through software, and fleets become distributed physical intelligence operating in the real world. cars are simply one of the first places where this transition can happen at enormous scale. the long term robotics revolution begins when we stop asking how to make existing machines autonomous and start asking what machines should look like when autonomy is assumed from first principles.

title:
The more I look into @axisrobotics, the more I think the real problem they’re solving isn’t robots.

It’s experience.

Think about how humans learn to do something new. We don’t just read instructions
content:
The more I look into @axisrobotics, the more I think the real problem they’re solving isn’t robots.

It’s experience.

Think about how humans learn to do something new. We don’t just read instructions and suddenly become good at it. We try, mess up, adjust, try again, and eventually get better.

Robots need that same kind of experience.

But giving physical robots millions of real-world attempts is expensive and painfully slow.

This is where Axis gets interesting.

Instead of relying entirely on physical robots, they let people interact with robots in simulation. Those interactions create trajectories that can be verified, cleaned up, and turned into useful training data.

Then the interesting part happens.

Mistakes and corrections don’t just get thrown away. They can become part of the learning process.

So you’re basically creating a loop where humans help generate experience, robots learn from it, and those lessons can produce better behavior.

That’s why the Booster experiment caught my attention too.

10 real demonstrations alone weren’t enough to get physical contact.

Add 50 simulation trajectories, and suddenly you’re looking at 17 successful contacts out of 20 trials.

That’s a pretty simple example of why simulation can matter so much.

For me, the bigger question isn’t how many trajectories Axis can collect.

It’s how much better those trajectories can make robots over time.

Because if you can build a system that keeps turning human experience into better robot behavior, you’re not just collecting data.

You’re building a feedback loop for Physical AI.

And that’s probably the part of axisrobotics worth watching

author: Jife790

title: One question that's been on my mind for years now is: could we use regular multimodal LLMs not necessarily trained for robotics to do the high level robotics intelligence part that VLAs and WAMs attem
content:
One question that's been on my mind for years now is: could we use regular multimodal LLMs not necessarily trained for robotics to do the high level robotics intelligence part that VLAs and WAMs attempt to do?

The latest explosion of powerful opensource multi-modal LLMs has, IMO, begun to make this possible due both to intelligence and speed. 

This is GLM 5.3 Flash, which has vision understanding, but isn't meant to be a VLA/VLM/WAM/robotics model at all, controlling an XGO mini wheeled robot quadruped with an arm & gripper.

GLM 5.3F simply has access to the robot's high level SDK for controlling movement, arm joints, open/close gripper...etc. It analyzes the frames from the camera and makes adjustments all on its own to solve the task.

Nothing was trained here, nothing fine-tuned for this task. Z AI did not make this model for robots and tbh I think they're surprised this works when I talk to them about it!

This also works quite well with DSV4F + a vision capable model like Qwen 3.8 27B. I havent tried JUST Qwen 3.8 27B, but I'm sure it works too. I like the "logic" to be a model that's as fast as possible (but still intelligent). There's also an experimental vision version of DSV4F, I'm confident that'll work too and might even be better bc the full loop might be the fastest of all with this model.

An obvious question you might wonder is: well why not use VLA or VLM? The hard part about robotics isn't object detection, that's long solved. This also isn't a solution for gait/locomotion...yet, but I actually don't think this is far away either and I've done some experimentation with LLMs in this space in the past and it does show promise.

It might actually already be here for quadrupeds, since you dont need super fast IMU readings to maintain balance. I've also tried many of the larger, more generalist, VLAs that you should be able to use with popular robots and tbh there are just so many edge cases that make things hard and not work. You gotta get the camera, lighting, task, everything *just right* or the demo fails. 

This is for the actual hard part in robotics right now: intelligence, logic, and planning for all the ways the real world just simply isn't perfect.

I've trained VLAs. They're super finicky and you're always running into sim2real issues, especially around the camera. You also have to build the whole training pipeline in a simulator, and, if everything does work, you still just have a robot that does this 1 single thing after weeks of work.

If you use teleop, this overcomes the "2real" problem, but now you need to painstakingly collect teleop data, and it's only good at that specific task and that particular robot. There is a growing set of egocentric training data for "general purpose" VLAs and world action models (for humanoid form factors), but I'm really starting to wonder: Why? I think we might just sidestep this whole area of research entirely. 

I didn't need any training data or special environment to work with this quadruped and arm to do the task I was after. This particular quadruped and arm doesn't even exist in the wild yet really, it's a demo build from a company launching it on kickstarter, so it's not like this robot's data exists in the LLM to any real extent.

I think this is cool as heck that this works and I am interested to see just how far I can push it. 

Also this marks the first time that I've finally got a generalist solution to a task I've been trying to solve ever since I became a dad of twins: pick up toys off the ground. This is a big day!

A robot learning to pick up a cup doesn't need one demonstration.

It needs to understand the task across thousands of variations:

↪ different cups.

↪ different positions.

↪ different lighting.

↪ different surfaces.

↪ different camera angles.

↪  different grasp points.

And eventually, the awkward edge cases that humans handle without even thinking.

The problem is obvious:

You can't put a human beside a physical robot and manually collect every possible variation.

That approach doesn't scale.

@axisrobotics attacks the problem differently.

Instead of treating robot data collection as a one-off recording exercise, Axis is building a system for manufacturing diverse robot experience.

It starts with the task.

Axis's Task Generation Engine can turn a desired behavior into structured, executable environments including objects, layouts, success conditions and randomization.

Those tasks can then be brought into simulation.

And simulation changes the economics completely.

A single task doesn't have to remain a single scenario.

Its objects, positions, appearances, lighting, camera viewpoints and other conditions can be varied to produce a much wider distribution of experiences.

Then Axis sends those tasks to its distributed contributor network.

People can interact with the simulated robots through the browser and generate trajectories without needing access to an expensive physical robot.

Every trajectory can then be replayed and verified before it becomes usable training data.

So the pipeline starts looking very different:

Task → Simulation → Human demonstration → Verification → Training data

But Axis doesn't stop there.

The data generated for one task can help improve the models.

Those models reveal new weaknesses.

Those weaknesses can define the next tasks.

And those tasks produce the next batch of data.

That's the beginning of the Compounding Data Engine.

Axis isn't simply asking:

“how do we collect more robot data?”

It's asking a much more important question:

“How do we build a system that gets better at producing the right robot data?”

That distinction could become critical as Physical AI moves from impressive demos to robots that have to operate reliably in the real world.

Because the future won't belong to the robots that have seen one million examples.

It may belong to the systems that know which one million examples should come next.

That's a wrap!

content:
Nvidia has completed its acquisition of Hugging Face. Why?

1/ Start with the price. In 2023, Hugging Face was valued at $4.5B. Earlier this year, Nvidia offered $7B to invest and was turned down. The acquisition now comes in at roughly $14B — exactly double what Nvidia itself had put on the table a few months earlier.

2/ The revenue multiple is even more striking. Hugging Face's annual revenue is around $150M. At $14B, that's over 80x annual revenue. That means this is something Nvidia had to push through.

3/ So what did they want that badly? I think the answer is Microduck.
Microduck isn't just a cute AI pet. It's a product built to collect physical AI training data and expand the ecosystem.

4/ The evidence is in the price. The 15 Robotis XL330 motors inside a Microduck cost $412 on their own, and it sells for $399. That's not thin margin — it's a loss. Proof it isn't a product meant to make money.

5/ The picture gets sharper when you look at what Nvidia has been saying all year. At CES 2026, Jensen Huang declared that the ChatGPT moment for physical AI had arrived. Appearing onstage with Olaf, he pointed to it and called this a $50 trillion industry. At GTC 2026 that followed, Nvidia announced its Physical AI Data Factory Blueprint, and the VP running Omniverse stated flatly that success comes down to whether you can generate massive amounts of data. The market is $50 trillion, and the fight is over data.

6/ So what Nvidia wants is millions of unpaid developers — ordinary people — learning physical AI while playing with a Microduck. The moment they start handling a robot, enormous volumes of training data start pouring out. For free.

7/ Physical AI requires robots to be deployed first. Only then does physical AI actually get applied and the robot's behavior change. Anyone following physical AI already knows that principle. The real question is how you deploy. You can't grow the developer base — ordinary people — with expensive robots. So they sold it below cost.

This is an enormous market. 
That's exactly why Hugging Face was worth paying double for. Microduck is a cultural movement Nvidia built to gather data.

So the pipeline becomes:

Generate → Demonstrate → Verify → Clean → Augment → Train → Correct → Retrain

The interesting part is that Axis is not simply trying to collect more data. It is building a system to continuously create better, more relevant data based on where the robot actually struggles.

That feedback loop could be a key piece in making robotics models more reliable in the real world.

content:
This is an interesting approach to robot learning.

Instead of collecting every training example by directly controlling a robot, X Square's TwinDEX lets humans demonstrate dexterous tasks using a wearable robotic hand.

The idea is pretty intuitive: if the wearable device and the robot are designed to work as a pair, the demonstrations can be transferred to the robot without having to collect everything on the robot itself.

And the tasks go beyond basic pick-and-place.

The demos include opening bottle caps, using a broom and dustpan, sliding and opening books, operating a syringe, and performing a multi-step chemistry experiment with more than 20 sub-actions.

The reported results show comparable learning efficiency between robot-free and on-robot data, while the robot-free setup achieved over 5× higher collection throughput.

It feels like a useful step toward making dexterous robot training data much easier to collect at scale.

content:
68 > 78.

That’s the number that keeps ringing in my head from Axis’ latest weekly.

Same evaluation >Three seeds >DAgger round two.

After adding the new correction set, the policy picked up roughly 10 more successes.

That might be a small number on paper, but it says a lot about how @axisrobotics is building its training loop.

The idea is simple: A human demonstrates a task >The policy tries to repeat it >When the policy slips, a human steps in and corrects it.

But Axis doesn’t just throw that entire human trajectory back into the dataset no. A takeover is capped at 8 steps, so the training data stays focused on the actual correction.

Then those corrections go into the next round, And the next round is already live (the sweetest part).

HG-DAgger candidates also moved 4-7 points above the source baseline.

Even the boring updates you see really matters here won’t lie. Undo no longer breaks replay, and verification is becoming less manual.

Honestly though if replay is wrong, the labels can be wrong too, And once bad data enters the loop, everything downstream gets even worse.

There’s still a weak spot, though. Because a policy can look great in Python and then lose performance when it reaches the browser runtime.

Axis called that out themselves and I Honestly like seeing that.

You don’t get to see a problem get solved completely every week, If the model is improving but the collection environment is now exposing the next problem, that’s useful information.

It means the loop is actually being tested correctly and this is why Hub matters.

I’m really paying close attention to this.

content:
hello my frens, happy Thursday 

This is exactly why I keep watching what @axisrobotics is building.

A man pushed a robot inside a tech store in Russia.

Seconds later, the robot appeared to push back, with the footage showing it moving toward the customer before people intervened.

Funny? Absolutely. 😂

But there’s a serious robotics lesson here.

Real world environments are unpredictable.

Robots won’t always get perfect conditions.

People will interfere with them. Objects will move unexpectedly. Tasks will fail. Environments will change.

And that raises an important question:

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘄𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗼𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗻'𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲?

This is where robotic training data becomes extremely important.

@axisrobotics is building infrastructure around exactly this problem, generating diverse robotic experiences in simulation, processing the data and using human feedback to improve robotic policies.

Because teaching a robot isn't simply about showing it how to succeed.

It also means giving it enough experience to understand what happens when things go wrong.

That’s one reason AXIS V2 is interesting to me.

Human corrections from failed or imperfect attempts can become useful training data for improving future iterations.

So while this video looks like a robot throwing hands lol, there’s a deeper lesson underneath it:

𝗥𝗼𝗯𝗼𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺.

That’s why the data layer matters. 🦾

content:
i was thinking about food delivery apps this morning.

having thousands of drivers is useful, but the real product is not “we have lots of drivers.”

it is the system that knows what needs picking up, where it should go, whether it arrived correctly and how to coordinate everything without the customer thinking about the machinery underneath.

robotics data feels surprisingly similar.

@axisrobotics has a distributed contributor layer, but its harder job is turning all that human activity into structured task sets and training data that an actual robotics team can use.

the recent Binance Wallet campaign gives more people another doorway into Axis tasks, which may help expand participation.

but personally i would not judge the project by how many people enter that doorway.

i would judge it by what eventually comes out the other side.

better datasets, repeatable workflows, useful sim2real results and customers willing to come back for another task set.

distribution can grow quickly.

operational quality is much harder to copy.

that is where i think the real Axis test sits.

content:
法クラ界隈でワークライフバランスがめちゃくちゃ話題になってますね。。

>「家族との時間をきちんと確保できる」というスタンスで仕事に向き合ってよいと思いますか。
>「1年365日...うまく工夫してプライベートの時間を作ることは可能です。ただ、それは恐らくご質問者が期待している「きちんと」というレベルには達しないように思います。大手の事務所に入るということはそういうことです。」
>「時短的な業務形態、育休など...あくまで各弁護士のライフイベントに応じた時限的なものに過ぎません。」

ライフやキャリアについての考えは完全に人それぞれ・事務所の方針それぞれだと思いますので、一つの考えとしてリスペクトしますし、また、実際問題として私自身も若い時のハードワークに現在非常に助けられていると感じます。

ただ、これはTRAを立ち上げた大きな理由の一つでもあるのですが、、ハードワークやハードワークの他者（これは同じ事務所の構成員であってもそうだと思います）への押し付けについては、『それによって何かを見失ってないか』とずっと感じていました。

法律事務所に限らないですが、プロファームでは、ハードワークを超え、ともするとサイコパス的な仕事の仕方や同僚への接し方、人間性の欠如が見受けられ、そういう人が出世していきます。

そして、「家族との時間をきちんと確保しない」というのは要するに家事や育児は全てパートナーに押し付けるという前提です（そして現代ではその負担が行くのは基本的に女性です）。

理想論でナイーブと言われるかもしれませんが、私自身は、「同僚に当たり前のように思いやりをもって接する」、「家事や育児は当たり前のようにパートナーと折半する」、そして、「人間性の向上や豊かな人生が仕事とのシナジーをもたらし正の循環を生む」、そういう組織を作りたいと思い、事務所を立ち上げました。

同僚の助けや、事務所で取り組んでいる業務効率化施策（Claudeのフル活用など）もあり、今のところ非常にうまく行っています。

創業以来、土日はほとんど仕事はせずに済んでいますし、平日も、朝の食事の用意・子供の送迎、夕刻は家族とのディナー・子供のお風呂など（子供の寝かしつけのあと夜1-2時間程度仕事はしますが）、家事・育児もパートナーとほぼイコールで折半できています。

それでも仕事のスピードやクオリティは落ちてないと自負しています。
無駄な仕事を減らす、仕事の効率化を図る、それで担保できると思うのです。そのためにAIを使うんじゃないでしょうか。

事務所のメンバーも同じ思いですし、みんな前職より、時間的余裕は増え、QOLは上がっていると言います（payという意味でも全員前職比で上がってます）。

人それぞれ・事務所それぞれですが、事務所立上げの理由に関わる部分ですので、コメントさせていただきました。

content:
【Physical AI】G20 Innovation Ministerial - Elon Muskが未来を語る
「既存の大企業という大木ではなく、スタートアップという小さな苗木を支援すべきだ」
さらに人型ロボットの価値を、
AI Software × AI Chip × Electromechanical Dexterity
と表現。この3つが指数関数的に進歩し、10年後には10億台以上の人型ロボットが存在すると予測した。

この視点でASIMO以降の日本を振り返ると、問題が見えてくる。
日本にはモーター、センサー、精密機械、制御など世界トップクラスの技術があった。しかし、それをAI・半導体・データと統合し、スタートアップを通じて高速に社会実装し、巨大なPhysical AI産業へ育てるエコシステムを十分作れなかった。

一方で米国はAI・半導体・VC・スタートアップを結合し、中国はさらに量産力・サプライチェーン・巨大市場を組み合わせて猛烈な速度で追い上げている。

だから日本に必要なのはASIMOは凄かったと振り返ることではない。
Research → Startup → Capital → Manufacturing → Deployment → Data → AI → Next Innovation
この循環を国内に作ること。

そしてMuskのDefault Legalという発想も重要だと思う。安全性を無視するのではなく、新しい技術をまず試せる制度を作り、問題が明確になったところをリスクベースで規制する。
AI時代の産業政策は「既存産業をどう守るか」から、「次の産業を生み出す苗木をどう増やすか」へ転換する必要がある。

content:
SK Hynixの大連のNAND工場からのeSSDは値上げ制限があったのか、これはタイミング悪すぎる

【ニュース】SKハイニックスの中国eSSD事業、インテルNAND取引制限が2026年末までに期限切れとなることで転換期を迎える

メモリブームによりDRAM、NAND、最終製品全体の価格が上昇する中、SKハイニックスは重要な成長転換点に近づいている。中国がSKハイニックスの企業向けSSD（eSSD）事業に課している5年間の規制が、2026年末に転換点を迎える見込みだと聯合ニュースが報じている。

中国におけるeSSD価格高騰への規制
DealSiteは、SKハイニックスの半期報告書を引用し、中国国家市場監督管理総局（SAMR）が2021年に同社によるインテルのNAND事業買収をいくつかの条件付きで承認したと報じた。主な制限事項はeSSDの価格設定に関するもので、取引条件が変更されないことを条件に、SKハイニックスは中国国内におけるPCIeおよびSATA eSSDの価格を承認前の24ヶ月間の平均価格以上に引き上げることを禁じられた、と同報告書は説明している。

聯合ニュースによると、今回の規制は、両社の合併が中国の企業向けSSD市場、特にPCIeおよびSATAインターフェースを使用する製品における競争を弱める可能性があるという国家市場監督管理総局（SAMR）の懸念に起因するものだという。

報告書によると、SKハイニックスは今後5年間、関連製品の生産を継続的に拡大し、中国のeSSD市場への第三の競合企業の参入を支援することも求められた。

SKハイニックスの5年間のコンプライアンス期間は今年12月に満了する予定だ。しかし、制限は自動的に解除されるわけではなく、同社は資格を満たした時点で解除を求める見込みだと聯合ニュースは報じている。制限が解除されれば、SKハイニックスは中国におけるeSSDの価格をAIデータセンターの需要やNANDフラッシュメモリ価格の上昇に合わせて調整する柔軟性が高まり、生産量やサプライヤーの割り当てを収益性に合わせて調整できるようになる。

SKハイニックスのNANDおよびeSSD事業における中国の戦略的役割
TrendForceによると、SKハイニックスにとって中国は重要なNAND生産拠点であり、2026年には同社のNAND生産能力全体の35～40％を中国が占めると予想されている。NANDチップはeSSDの基盤となるため、この中国における生産能力は同社のグローバルなAIサーバー供給を支えており、こうした現地価格の上限が撤廃される可能性は、同社の収益性にとって極めて重要な起爆剤となるだろう。

こうした背景の中、SKハイニックスもeSSD市場でますますプレッシャーにさらされている。TrendForceによると、 Solidigmを含むSKハイニックスグループは、2026年第2四半期にeSSDの世界市場シェア21.1%で2位となり、第1四半期の23.1%から低下した。サムスンは35.1%のシェアで首位を維持し、Micronは17.1%で3位となり、第1四半期の15.4%から上昇した。

中国のeSSD競争がSAMRの決定に影響を与える可能性
聯合ニュースによると、中国当局は規制解除の判断にあたり、AIデータセンターの顧客に対し安定した費用対効果の高い供給を確保する必要性と、YMTCのような国内企業を育成する取り組みとのバランスを取らなければならない。

YMTCはNAND市場での地位を急速に強化し、最近では世界のリーダー企業に迫っている。エンタープライズ向けSSDは依然として同社の事業のごく一部を占めるに過ぎないが、eSSD事業の拡大は重要な成長の原動力となる可能性があると聯合ニュースは報じている。YMTCをはじめとする中国企業が存在感を強めるにつれ、国家市場監督管理総局（SAMR）は市場競争が現在の規制緩和を正当化するほど十分に活発になったと判断する可能性があると、同報道は説明している。

同時に、こうした規制を維持することは、別のジレンマを生み出す可能性もある。SKハイニックスに課せられた価格上限は、同社を制約するだけでなく、中国のeSSDメーカーの価格競争力と収益性にも圧力をかける可能性があると、聯合ニュースは指摘している。これは、国内サプライヤーを支援する必要性と市場競争のバランスを取る上で、国家市場監督管理総局（SAMR）の決定をさらに複雑にする可能性がある。

title:
有料フォントをAIが学習したら権利侵害！？……いやッ！！そこ一緒にしちゃダメだろッ！！

「あー……生成AIって、有料フォントで作った画像も学習してるから危険なのか……」って話、ちょっと待ってほしいッ！！「有料フォントそのもの」と「そのフォントで描いた文字画像」は同じものじゃないッ！！そこ混ぜたら話がめちゃくちゃになるだろッ！！

⭐️有料フォントって「文字の画像」だけじゃないッ！！

有料フォン
content:
有料フォントをAIが学習したら権利侵害！？……いやッ！！そこ一緒にしちゃダメだろッ！！

「あー……生成AIって、有料フォントで作った画像も学習してるから危険なのか……」って話、ちょっと待ってほしいッ！！「有料フォントそのもの」と「そのフォントで描いた文字画像」は同じものじゃないッ！！そこ混ぜたら話がめちゃくちゃになるだろッ！！

⭐️有料フォントって「文字の画像」だけじゃないッ！！

有料フォントでまず大事なのは、.otfとか.ttfみたいなフォントデータなんだよッ！！何千文字もの字形に、字幅、カーニング、置換規則なんかまで入った「文字を表示するためのデータ一式」なのッ！！

文化庁の資料でも、「書体そのもの」と「フォントプログラム」は分けて考えられてる。なのに「有料フォントで描いた文字が画像に入ってた！有料フォントそのものだ！」って……ならないッ！！ならないんだよォッ！！

⭐️PNGになった文字はフォントファイルじゃないッ！！

たとえば1万円のフォントで「生成AIについて考える」って書いてPNGにする。そのPNGを見た人が……1万円のフォントを無断使用したことになるの！？ならんだろッ！！怖すぎるだろそんな世界ッ！！

フォントってそもそも、文字を表示して、本やポスターや画像みたいな成果物を作るために売られてるものなんだよッ！！成果物に文字が描かれてるだけで、フォントファイルまで配布されたことにはならないッ！！

⭐️フォント持ってない人も成果物は見られるんだよッ！！

モリサワだって、正規ライセンスで作ったアウトライン化・画像化された成果物について、フォントを持っていない第三者が利用できる場合があるって説明してる。そりゃそうだろッ！！本を読む人全員にフォント買わせるのかよッ！！

ただし、文字画像を大量に用意して「はい、この画像を組み合わせればフォント買わなくても全部の文字が使えます！」みたいにしたら話が変わる。だってもう……フォントの代用品を作ってるじゃんッ！！

⭐️「書体の形」なら全部著作権！！でもないッ！！

さらに日本では、書体の形そのものに普通のイラストと同じような著作権が当然についてくるわけでもないッ！！最高裁のゴナU事件でも、印刷用書体が著作物になる条件にはかなり高いハードルが置かれてる。

従来の書体と比べて顕著な特徴があって、それ自体が美術鑑賞の対象になるような美的特性まで必要とされてる。だから「有料フォントっぽい文字が出たァ！！著作権侵害だァ！！」って……そんな単純じゃないッ！！

⭐️画像を学習するのとフォントをコピーするのは別ッ！！

生成AIが、有料フォントで文字が書かれたポスターや画像を学習する。その中から文字の形について統計的な特徴を学んで、似た雰囲気の文字を画像として出す。それと「OTFファイルをコピーしました」は別の行為だろッ！！

モリサワのフォントで書かれた大量のポスターをAIが見て、「未来」っていう二文字を似たゴシック体で描いた。それだけでモリサワのOTFファイルを複製したことになるの！？……ならんッ！！話が飛びすぎなんだよォッ！！

⭐️本当に危なくなるのは「フォント丸ごと再現」だろッ！！

逆に危なくなってくるのは、特定の有料フォントについて、ひらがな、カタカナ、英数字、漢字を大量に体系的に生成して、「これ並べたら元フォント買わなくても使えるじゃん！」ってところまで行った場合。

そこまで行ったら単なる文字画像じゃないッ！！実質的に「フォント製品の代用品」を作ってる方向に近づく。そうなったらフォントベンダーの規約や著作権、その他の権利までちゃんと検討する必要が出てくるッ！！

⭐️コピー！学習！生成！再構築！全部一緒にするなァッ！！

フォントファイルをコピーする。フォントで描かれた画像を見る・学習する。似た字形を画像として生成する。さらにフォント一式を丸ごと再現して代替品を作る。……全部違う行為なんだよッ！！

なのに「有料フォントで作った画像が学習データに入ってる！だからAI文字生成は一番リスキー！」って……いやァァッ！！途中の話ぜんぶ吹っ飛ばしてるッ！！問題になるなら、単発の文字より「フォント丸ごと代替できるほど再現した場合」だろッ！！

⭐️生成AIの著作権問題、だいたい同じところで混乱してるッ！！

この話、画像生成AIでずっと揉めてる「作品を学習すること」と「作品そのものを再現すること」の区別とかなり似てる。学習データに作品があったというだけで、生成された画像が自動的に元作品のコピーになるわけじゃない。

文化庁だってAIと著作権について、学習段階と生成・利用段階を分けて整理してるんだよッ！！フォントだって同じッ！！「何を学習した！？」だけで叫ぶんじゃなくて、「最終的に何をコピー・生成・再現した！？」まで分けて考えようよォッ！！

アンバサダー様には、無理のない範囲で

・コラボ配信へのご協力

コラボグッズ制作も予定しております！

企画に関しては、すべての企画へ

募集形式でご案内し、

content:
「Cowork × Fable 5.1」と「Work × GPT-5.6 Sol」で、スライド生成を比較しました。

Fable 5.1（左）
・情報の扱い：データに基づく緻密な分析と密度の高い情報量
・デザイン ：複雑なグラフや詳細な表を用いた、実務的なレイアウト

GPT-5.6 Sol（右）
