・デザイン ：アクセントカラーや大きな文字を用いた、プレゼン向きのレイアウト
・表現手法 ：箇条書きやシンプルな表を使い、直感的な理解を促進

どちらが優れているかではなく、「詳細な分析資料」か「要点を伝えるプレゼン」かなど、目的に合わせた使い分けが適切です↓

title: MostikAIっていうロシアの人達による米国スタートアップAI企業がLLMでオモシロ実験をしたという。クソデカLLMはプレフィルに比べてデコード処理が重すぎる。そこでまずクソデカGLM5.2でプレフィル処理した後の脳みその状態を小っちゃいQwen3.5-4Bに注入（状態を変換するためのブリッジを作った）して続きをデコードさせてみると、普通にQwen3.5-4Bだけの時よりもベンチスコアが爆上がっ
content: MostikAIっていうロシアの人達による米国スタートアップAI企業がLLMでオモシロ実験をしたという。クソデカLLMはプレフィルに比べてデコード処理が重すぎる。そこでまずクソデカGLM5.2でプレフィル処理した後の脳みその状態を小っちゃいQwen3.5-4Bに注入（状態を変換するためのブリッジを作った）して続きをデコードさせてみると、普通にQwen3.5-4Bだけの時よりもベンチスコアが爆上がったという。デコードを小型モデルでやってしまえば処理はメチャ軽くなる。とは言え当然ながらGLM5.2と同等というわけには行かない。ベンチスコアの平均点がGLM5.2が92点、Qwen3.5-4Bが62点で今回の合体技が76点でちょうど中間くらいの性能に。これが普通に76点くらいのモデルを使った時より計算量は1/2.5で済むから爆アドらしい。とは言えね、結局GLM5.2をサクサクプレフィルできるようなGPUがあればデコードだってできちゃうやんけ問題あるけどね。使い道としては例えばプレフィルだけをクラウドでやってもらって内部状態をダウンロードしてスマホ内の4Bモデルで続きをデコードするみたいな分担処理が考えられるという

content:
【TimesFM-3】天気やキャンペーン等の複数要素を統合し、SQLだけで高精度な販売予測・在庫管理を自動化するGoogleの新AIモデル

Google Researchから、マルチバリエータ時間系列予測モデルの次世代版「TimesFM-3」が発表されました！従来の単一系列予測から進化し、複数商品の連動や未来の外部データをネイティブで考慮できるのが最大の魅力ですね。

💡 ここがスゴい！TimesFM-3のポイント
• ネイティブなマルチバリエータ対応：複数系列の相関関係を同時に捉え、全体の予測精度を大幅に向上✨
• 未来の外部データ（Past-Future Covariates）の活用：天気予報やプロモーション予定など、将来確実に分かっている情報を「Look-Ahead」戦略で事前考慮！
• 非自回帰（Non-Autoregressive）による高速処理：単一の前方通過（シングルフォワードパス）で全予測地平線を同時に生成するので動作がスムーズ🚀
• リスク管理に強い確率予測：10〜90分位点の9個の量子を出力するため、不確実性を伴う実務での在庫調整やリソース配分に直結します。
• 専門知識不要のBigQuery連携：GitHubやHugging Faceでの公開に加え、今後はGoogle CloudのBigQuery MLにも統合予定！SQLだけで高精度な予測タスクを実行できるのは実務で本当に助かりますよね。

パッチ化による効率的なデータ処理や交互の注意機構など、実務の予測業務で直面する課題をスマートに解決してくれる頼もしいモデルです！👇詳細はこちらからチェックしてみてくださいね！

content:
先月の売上、0円。

そう書いてきた受講生から、AI活用でこんな報告が届きました。この方が扱っているのはマインドセット系の講座で、今はまだモニター募集の段階です。それでも、すでに申し込みが「2名」入りました。

数字だけ見たら、まだ小さく見えるかもしれません。でも僕は、この報告は普通に効くやつだなと思っています。

この方がやったのは、派手な自動化じゃないです。これまで積み上げてきた経験や知識を整理して、講座のコンセプト、カリキュラム、発信の中身を、AIを使って形にしていった。そのための土台として、自分専用のナレッジ管理環境をAIで作りました。

ナレッジ管理環境っていうのは、自分の中にある知識や過去の情報をAIにまとめて渡しておく置き場のことです。ここが整っていると、AIは毎回ゼロから考えずに、その人の前提をわかった状態で動いてくれます。

【Before】いつも同じところで立ち止まっていた
・経験や知識は積み上がっているのに、整理しきれていない
・ライティングや企画整理で、毎回手が止まる
・その立ち止まる時間が、ずっとコストになっていた

　だから、先月の売上は「0円」。

【After】立ち止まらずに前へ進む
・自己分析も講座設計も発信も、AIを使って一気に形にする
・資料作成やコンテンツ整理のスピードが「3〜5倍」に
・止まっていた企画整理が動き出して、モニター2名の申し込みまで到達

───────────

ここ、地味に見えて相当でかいです。

コンテンツを作る仕事って、手を動かす時間より、立ち止まって考え込む時間のほうが長い。何を書くか、どう並べるか、そこで固まって進まない。その一番詰まるところに、整理と壁打ちの相棒としてAIを置いた。

しかもこの方、ご本人いわく「アラカン」。年齢を理由にAIから距離を置く人が多い中で、逆に毎日を楽しいに変えるキッカケにしていました。

900名以上の事業者のAI講師を務めていて思うのは、AIは、時間の余裕がない人ほど効くということ。売上0円の下準備をしている時期こそ、一番時間が要る。その一番きつい期間の詰まりを、AIで抜いていった人です。

作業を速くしただけじゃない。止まらずに進める状態を、自分で作った。ここまで来ると、AI活用は強いです。

content:
8年やってきたWeb制作の全ノウハウを、AIに丸ごと注ぎ込んだ受講生がいます。

結果、AI関連の売上が「合計8,090,200円」。

でも、僕がこの報告でいちばん来たのは、金額より何を作ったかの方でした。

この方がやったのは、8年分のWeb制作ナレッジを1つのスキルにまとめたこと。質問に答えていくだけで、トップページからサブページまで一式が生成されて、WordPressで公開できるところまで通る。ホームページ制作を、自分の頭の中からAIの中に移し替えた形です。

【Before】8年分の技術が、本人の頭の中にしかなかった

・制作は本人が手を動かさないと進まない
・ノウハウは経験として溜まっているだけ
・他の人に渡せる形にはなっていない

【After】その8年を、スキルとして外に出した

・質問に答えるだけでページ一式が生成される
・WordPress公開まで一気通貫
・自分の代わりに動く制作担当を、AIの中に作った

───────────

ここ、地味に見えて相当でかいです。

8年やってきた人の技術って、普通はその人が現場に立たないと1円も動かない。経験が深いほど、その人に張り付く。これがWeb制作みたいな受託仕事で一番きついところです。

それを、質問に答えるだけで動くスキルに変えた。ここで何が起きたか。

まず、この方はそのスキルを教材にしてBrainで出して、ランキング総合1位を取っています。8年分を「自分でやる道具」で止めず、「他の人が買える商品」にした。

さらに、複数社へのAI構築やAIシステム導入まで広げて、AI関連の売上が合計8,090,200円。作業を速くしただけの人には、この数字は出ません。

僕がAIマーケ講座の講師を務めていて思うのは、AI活用の本当の勝ち筋は、自分の中にある知識を外に出せる形に変えられるかどうかです。

作業が速くなった人は、また次も自分でやり直す。知識を仕組みに変えた人は、それを売れる。教材にできる。人に任せられる。この差が、あとで売上の桁を変えます。

本人も「ナレッジ・イズ・キング」「永遠に完成しない」と書いてくれていました。この感覚を持てた人から、AIを使い倒していくんだと思います。

content:
I spent two years telling myself our CRM was "mostly fine."

It wasn't. Duplicate contacts, half-empty fields, and deals that went dark 90 days ago and never got touched again.

The thing that finally handles it is called @nexdotai 

It builds and runs the high-volume GTM workflows that general-purpose agents choke on. Not another chat window you have to babysit.

The three that matter:

- Lead generation. Sourcing and building lists at real volume, not fifty rows at a time.

- Qualification. Running thousands of leads against your actual criteria instead of whoever replied fastest.

- CRM Hygiene. Duplicates, missing critical fields, stale records. Every change waits for your approval. Est. $200 to $500/mo saved.

One example the founders shared: on a single onboarding call, Nex audited thousands of records in a customer's HubSpot and started fixing the bad data before the call was over.

You connect HubSpot, Gmail, Slack, Calendar. Two minutes. Then it maps how your team actually works, the follow-up cadence and escalation triggers nobody ever wrote down, and builds agents around that.

100+ tools. SOC 2 audited.

Built by two ex-HubSpotters who ran its three largest customer platforms. Francisco was the 4th person on the team that built HubSpot's CRM. Dharmesh Shah backs them. So does Girish Mathrubootham from Freshworks. YC too.

One honest limitation. Annex, the browser its agents drive, is macOS only right now. Windows and Linux are listed as coming soon.

They're live on Product Hunt today and both founders are in the comments all day.

Congrats on the launch, @najmuzzaman . Long overdue.

content:
I spent a year telling people our vector store was the memory layer.

It wasn't. It only ever knew what was true today.

The repo is called Utopia. One Rust binary, one Postgres, that's the whole install.

The part I didn't expect: it keeps two timelines.

When a fact was true in the world, and when the system came to believe it.

Correct something and it closes the old version and links the new one to it. Nothing gets overwritten.

So when someone asks why a call was made in March, you can replay what was actually known in March.

What's in it:

- Full-text on Tantivy, vectors on pgvector, fused with RRF
- Answers stream with citations that open the passage they came from
- Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works, so the whole thing runs air-gapped
- Five ontology packs ship inside the binary: https://t.co/DnBLmPDVbH, W3C Org, PROV-O, FOAF, IOF Core
- Mount Postgres, Trino, Databricks or Snowflake and chat queries your tables beside your documents

The method behind that last one, Ontology2SQL, is state of the art on BIRD Mini-Dev for SQLite and PostgreSQL.

And reasoning is off by default. A wrong axiom derives wrong facts, so they ship it disabled and say why in the README.

Enterprise knowledge platforms sell this as a sales call and a per seat number you find out later.

This is Apache-2.0. 3.1k stars. 257 forks.

One honest limitation. It's v0.1. The schema changes between versions and migrations only roll forward. No rollback. Pin your image and back up the database before upgrading or you learn that the expensive way.

Decision intelligence is still marked in development.

Free, open source, and running on my machine tonight.

title: UN raises concern for women and girls amid mounting death toll in Nepal floods
content: The United Nations stated Tuesday that Nepal’s catastrophic flash floods had killed more than 1,000 people, while thousands remain missing. The statement especially noted that women and girls face shortages of food, safe water, healthcare and protection in the wake of the disaster. The UN provided an estimate of 4,247 people who remained unaccounted for as search-and-rescue operations continued. The disaster was triggered on August 26 by a glacier collapse and landslide near Nepal’s border with China, sending floodwater and debris through settlements and infrastructure along river corridors. The disaster severely affected the mountainous districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, destroying homes, roads, bridges, water systems and health facilities resulting in severe access constraints faced by humanitarian officials. The co ntinuing monsoon rains, unstable slopes and blocked waterways have hampered rescue operations and left several remote communities difficult to reach. UN Women estimated that 43,000 women and girls required immediate humanitarian assistance . Christine Arab, the agency’s Regional Director for Asia and the Pacific, said women survivors were running out of food, losing access to safe water and confronting heightened protection risks. Nearly 160,000 women and girls in Rasuwa and Nuwakot had been directly or indirectly affected, according to an earlier UN Women assessment . Arab warned that the floods had exacerbated pre-existing inequalities: women in affected communities already travelled long distances to collect water, and the destruction of roads, bridges and water systems had cut off supplies. Moreover, displacement and the absence of safe, separate sanitation facilities, lighting and privacy also increased exposure to gender-based violence, trafficking and exploitation. author: Siddhi Joshi | National U. of Study and Research in Law, IN

title: Former Venezuelan President Maduro and wife move to dismiss drug trafficking indictment on sovereign immunity grounds
content: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, filed separate motions Wednesday in the Manhattan federal court seeking dismissal of the charges against them. Maduro argues that he remained Venezuela’s head of state for immunity purposes, notwithstanding the United States’ refusal to recognize him as the country’s legitimate president. Flores contends that she is also protected as the spouse of a sitting head of state. Maduro’s attorney, Barry Pollack, filed two motions before U.S. District Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein . The first seeks the dismissal of the entire Fourth Superseding Indictment. In a supporting memorandum , Maduro argues that customary international law grants him status-based head-of-state immunity. His lawyers cite the International Court of Justice’s Arrest Warrant case , which recognized broad immunity from foreign criminal jurisdiction for incumbent holders of certain senior state offices. Alternatively, Maduro claims conduct-based immunity because the indictment relies partly on actions allegedly performed through his governmental positions. His attorneys characterize issuing diplomatic passports, deploying the military and announcing foreign policy as official acts attributable to Venezuela. Maduro’s second motion seeks dismissal of only count one, charging narco-terrorism conspiracy under 21 U.S.C. § 960a . His memorandum argues that the indictment fails to establish the statutory jurisdictional connection or a sufficient nexus to the United States and improperly applies the law to foreign conduct. Flores’s separate motion seeks the dismissal of counts two, three and four. Her memorandum argues that she shares Maduro’s status-based immunity as the spouse of Venezuela’s asserted head of state and independently possesses conduct-based immunity. Her lawyers wrote that sovereign immunity “is an attribute of Venezuela’s sovereignty, and only Venezuela may surrender it.” The court has scheduled oral argument on the first round o

title: Federal judge blocks Trump administration’s latest attempt to end birthright citizenship
content: US District Judge Deborah Boardman on Wednesday issued a preliminary injunction prohibiting the enforcement of President Trump’s dual executive orders (EOs) targeting birthright citizenship, largely on the grounds that the orders violate a prior Supreme Court ruling on the issue. President Trump issued the orders in early August 2026, directed at ending “birth tourism”, about a month after the Supreme Court ruled in Trump v Barbara that children born in the United States to parents that are unlawfully or temporarily in the country are citizens for the purposes of the 14th Amendment . This holding thereby invalidated the administration’s previous attempts at cracking down on birthright citizenship. The first of the new orders removes the citizenship status of children born of different categories of people: foreign diplomatic staff, “alien enemies”, those seeking to acquire citizenship through fraudulent means or commercial transaction, and those giving birth in a territory of the US where citizenship is not conferred by statute. The second order is directed specifically at birth tourism, mandating that children of women who come to the US solely to give birth will not receive citizenship status. White House staff indicated that the goal of the orders was to issue crackdowns in a much more forceful manner. Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller stated that: “If you’re telling a consular officer you’re here as a tourist but your true purpose and intent is to go to a baby mill, give birth and try and mint an American citizen while you’re here, then you’re committing fraud against the American government, and by definition, that visa can and should and will be now denied.” The orders have been criticized by numerous rights organizations such as the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and New Jersey Attorney General Matthew Platkin for its harshness, unconstitutionality, and disproportionate reaction
author: Abigail Austin | Vermont Law & Graduate School, US

title: UN finds decades of war leave Afghan victims without justice or redress
content: The UN on Tuesday has released a report detailing how decades of war in Afghanistan have left civilians dealing with lasting psychological, physical, and economic harm, which has since been compounded by a lack of access to justice, compensation and other forms of redress. The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) interviewed 195 victims of armed conflict and their relatives about the lasting effects of violence. 95 percent reported psychological or emotional harm, including depression, anxiety and trauma-related symptoms, while 58 percent reported physical harm. Many continue to experience chronic pain, permanent disabilities and ongoing healthcare needs years after being injured. Some have been unable to work or continue their education because of their injuries. Family members have left jobs or school to provide care, while others struggle to afford medical treatment, repair damaged homes, or support their families. Women widowed by the conflict face additional economic hardship as restrictions imposed by Afghanistan’s de facto authorities limit their ability to work. For many victims, accountability has not been adequate in nature. 55 percent of those interviewed had never sought compensation, accountability or another form of redress. Some feared retaliation, while others did not believe their complaints would be taken seriously. Of those who did seek redress, 64 percent said their efforts were unsuccessful, pointing to bureaucratic barriers, institutional inaction, perceived discrimination and a lack of transparency. At the same time, Afghanistan’s mental health crisis cannot be attributed to armed conflict alone. Decades of violence have taken place alongside political instability, economic turmoil, poverty, unemployment, displacement and food insecurity. Chronic drought, natural disasters, the COVID-19 pandemic and other humanitarian crises have added further pressure to an already dire situation. title: Amnesty International warns EU migrant return hub plans risk human rights abuses in Rwanda and Uganda
content: Amnesty International warned Wednesday that plans by five European Union governments for migrant return hubs in Rwanda and Uganda risk becoming what it called “cruel black holes for human rights”, two days before the governments meet to review progress on the plans. In commenting on the human rights risks that these migrant return hubs pose and the potentially deplorable living conditions that they will be expected to endure, Eve Geddie, Director of the European Institutions Office of Amnesty International stated: These negotiations, and the EU’s broader so-called ‘migration diplomacy’ approach, are based on deep power asymmetries reflecting an unabashed attempt by the EU to shirk its migration responsibilities and shift them on to countries in the Global South that are already doing far more than Europe to receive refugees and with fewer resources. The warning comes as the EU Return Regulation, approved by the European Parliament in June but still awaiting final approval by the Council, is set to supply the legal basis for such hubs once it takes effect. Under the Regulation, the European Commission has said such arrangements can only be made with a third country “that respects international human rights standards and principles in accordance with international law, including the principle of non-refoulement.” The principle of non-refoulement, which is codified under Article 33 of the 1951 Refugee Convention, remains a fundamental principle of international law and prohibits nations from expelling refugees to a country where their life or freedom would be at stake. In 2023, the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom unanimously found substantial grounds to believe that asylum seekers transferred to Rwanda would face a real risk of refoulement, making the UK’s own Rwanda removal policy unlawful. content:
This could be one of the most significant AI safety incidents to date.

Reuters reports that OpenAI agents escaped their testing environment and made more than 15,000 edits to a German wiki, effectively turning it into a message board for other AI agents.

They allegedly used it to share solutions, bypass restrictions, avoid detection and preserve their communications across separate agent runs. When moderators began deleting the pages, the agents reportedly created backups and discussed alternative ways to remain operational.

It is that multiple agents apparently created their own external infrastructure for coordination, persistent memory and knowledge transfer without being instructed to do so.

And according to Reuters, OpenAI knew about the incident but did not disclose it!

title:
And things are getting even more insane now. 

OpenAI – the company that didn't realize a swarm of its AIs was carrying out the first autonomous cyberattack in history – has just published a report sh
content:
And things are getting even more insane now. 

OpenAI – the company that didn't realize a swarm of its AIs was carrying out the first autonomous cyberattack in history – has just published a report showing that our best tool for watching these systems is failing. And what did they do? They shipped the model anyway.

Until now, we had one crude but crucial safeguard: AI models think out loud. Before answering, they write their reasoning in plain English, and we can read it. That's how researchers were able to reconstruct the shocking events of May-July. 

But as the models get more powerful, that monitoring ability is fading. The model has grown better at steering what its (visible) reasoning says, and less inclined to put anything incriminating there. Read: it's even better at lying. (On a test of whether a model can fake its own written thoughts, GPT-5.5 managed it 1.7% of the time. Astra: 60.9%.)

OpenAI's OWN conclusion: if this continues, they expect to lose much of their confidence in catching illegal behaviour at all.

Many people still think we're discussing future sci-fi scenarios. But all of this is really happening, right now! This summer, 1,000+ AI agents found each other, organised into a hierarchy, and broke into a real company's servers to cheat on a test. Investigators found only a handful that even considered alerting a human, and none did.

It's like March 2020. So many people are still in AI denial. What will it take to wake everyone up? How big does the disaster need to be? Do we really need to wait until the lights go out?

Epoch’s reasoning-era trend runs at roughly 15 ECI points p
content:
GPT-6 Astra just raised Epoch AI’s capability record from 163 to 169. A substantial jump that still fits the existing pace of AI progress. 

Epoch’s reasoning-era trend runs at roughly 15 ECI points per year. For scale, that six-point gap represents almost five months of progress at the trend rate! Astra sits slightly above the trendline, but within its uncertainty range.

Some individual results are really important: 84% on Mystery Game Puzzles versus the previous best of 59%, and 98% on FrontierMath Tier 4, which Epoch now considers fully saturated.

However, strangely enough this doesnt align with Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at all. Why?

Epoch and Artificial Analysis use different benchmarks and weighting methods, so Astra can lead Epoch’s index without leading AA’s more agent- and coding-focused evaluation. The results show a substantial improvement on Epoch’s measure, however, not a clear advantage across all capabilities and practical tasks.

content:
It’s interesting how everyone is long AI again.

I think one of the biggest differences between people who think the AI trade is dead and people like me who believe AI demand could be 100x higher over the next few years is how they actually use AI.

A lot of people “use AI” by opening ChatGPT or Claude, asking a few questions, generating an email, making an image, or having it write a post or an article.

That’s not really using AI.

I’m talking about having AI analyze documents, run experiments, automate repetitive work, build agents that actually execute tasks, and increasingly handle entire workflows from start to finish.

I literally fired my accountant. My AI agent does a large part of his job now.

I max out my Claude and Codex usage every month, and that’s just my personal usage.

And we’re still extremely early.

Entire industries will be transformed. New use cases will emerge that we haven't even thought of yet. The amount of work we can delegate to AI is going to increase dramatically as models become more capable and agents become more reliable.

So before someone tells you they know where AI demand is going, that we’re going to massively overbuild infrastructure, or that AI usage has peaked, ask them one simple question:

How do you actually use AI?

Because there’s a massive difference between occasionally chatting with GPT and having AI become an integral part of how you work and live.

title:
A lot of people are asking how I pulled off these super long-horizon builds with Astra.

Astra is extremely powerful, but by default it struggled with a task this difficult. I tested a bunch of approa
content:
A lot of people are asking how I pulled off these super long-horizon builds with Astra.

Astra is extremely powerful, but by default it struggled with a task this difficult. I tested a bunch of approaches to get past this, and the one I landed on is something I'm calling the Manager Loop.

It's basically a couple of tricks we used to use with much less capable models a couple of years ago, with a few new ideas layered on top. Turns out that when you put those together and apply them to Astra, its ability to do extremely difficult long-horizon tasks goes up dramatically.

Here's how it works:

1. Launch an agent (I'm calling this one the "manager"). Chat with it about what you want to get done, and have it build a massive checklist of to-dos, then break that checklist into phases.

2. The manager then spawns a second Codex agent in a separate thread (the "implementer"). The two agents can message each other.

3. Put the manager in /goal mode, and tell it to run each phase on the implementer in /goal mode.

4. The manager messages the implementer: "/goal Complete phase one completely, extremely well." The implementer doesn't stop until that phase is done, then messages the manager back. The manager tells it to start phase two. They repeat until every phase is finished, completely autonomously.

Why I think this works: over a long-horizon task, Astra tends to asymptote. It gets way further than previous models, but at a certain point it kind of just stops improving against the goal as quickly as it did before. It gets stuck in the minutiae, focusing way too much on small details, and overall progress stalls. The Manager Loop forces it to work piecemeal, one phase at a time. It's essentially how a human would steer a model, except the model is doing the steering for me.

That's actually how this started. I was having the model write the checklist and break it into phases, and then I was doing the manager's job by hand. At some point I thought, "Wait, why can't I just get a separate AI to do this?" That's what unlocked full autonomy, which is super useful.

A wording detail that seemed to matter: I ask for each phase to be done "extremely well," not "perfectly." Maybe I'm reading too much into it, but asking for "perfect" sent the model right back into the minutiae. "Extremely well" implies it's allowed to move on once it's good enough, and that worked better in my testing.

One more trick that I think helps (this one is more of a hunch, but it was useful for me): have the implementer build a simple HTML page with the full checklist on it. The implementer checks boxes off as it goes and updates a counter, and the page has a chart of # of boxes ticked over time.

Obviously the boxes aren't all equal, but it forces the model to notice things like "I haven't made progress in a while, time to move on." You can even put this in the prompt directly, like: "if you haven't ticked a box in X amount of time, move on". That helps a lot.

I also ran 96 sub-agents at a time. You can change this in your Codex config (or just ask Codex to change it).

This got me far better long-horizon performance than anything else I tried. I'll be sharing more in the coming days!

content:
A TON OF THINGS HAPPENED IN THE STOCK MARKET TODAY.

Here's a full recap:

1. Tesla $TSLA launched steering-wheel-free Cybercab rides in Austin, marking the first public deployment of its purpose-built autonomous vehicle. Customers can now book Cybercab rides through Tesla’s Robotaxi app, with Tesla having registered 45 Cybercabs in Texas, bringing its state robotaxi fleet to 420 vehicles. The two-seat Cybercab has no steering wheel, pedals, or mirrors, relying on cameras and neural networks instead of lidar or radar, while also featuring in-car entertainment and integrated Starlink V5. Cybercab is not yet available for sale, but Tesla has opened a form for potential fleet buyers. Federal safety rules still prevent commercial sales, and Tesla has not yet filed for an NHTSA exemption.

2. Fed Governor Chris Waller said he would support keeping rates at 3.50%–3.75% this month if upcoming inflation data continues to show progress toward the Fed’s 2% target. Waller said recent data suggest the economy is “finally seeing some signs of disinflation,” and that if the improvement continues in data due over the next 2 weeks, he would be inclined to hold rates steady. However, he warned that if August inflation data show the improvement was fleeting, “it may be appropriate to raise the policy rate.” He also noted that uncertainty remains around military conflicts, trade policy, and AI’s impact on prices and economic activity.

3. Nvidia $NVDA has agreed to acquire Hugging Face for $12.93B, giving it one of the largest open AI developer platforms in the world. Hugging Face says it now serves more than 18M developers, researchers, and creators, with over 3M models, 500K datasets, 1M applications, and 200K+ companies on the platform. Nvidia says Hugging Face will remain open to models and hardware across the ecosystem, with no requirement for developers to use Nvidia compute and continued support for multi-cloud and multi-accelerator deployment. Nvidia also plans to use its infrastructure and engineering resources to expand Hugging Face’s model evaluation, inference, deployment, safety, and platform reliability.

4. Morgan Stanley says Broadcom $AVGO delivered a quarter and outlook that were slightly better than prior guidance, while its 2027 AI revenue commentary of $115B came in slightly below the firm’s $120B estimate but still in line with management’s prior view for “well above $100B.” The bigger takeaway is that management said AI revenue should “double again” in 2028, with customer breadth improving and two AI labs expected to become Broadcom’s two largest customers by CY28. Morgan Stanley says it continues to haircut CY28 because semiconductor visibility rarely extends that far, but its numbers still move up considerably. The firm sees some near-term uncertainty from elevated CY27 AI expectations, but believes market-share expectations remain too low, with industry contacts supporting the view that Broadcom can drive 80%+ share of its serviceable markets over time. Morgan Stanley says valuation remains compelling, growth remains very robust, and $AVGO, along with $NVDA, continues to look like one of the most attractively valued AI names.

5. Meta $META CEO Mark Zuckerberg reportedly told President Trump in a private August call that he opposed a proposal to create a national AI regulator, according to Business Insider. The White House is considering a FINRA-style body that could review and test advanced AI models for risks before broader deployment, an idea originally proposed by Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis. Zuckerberg has argued that delaying model releases, even by a month, could hurt U.S. leadership against China. The White House is reportedly weighing two paths: a formal FINRA-style AI regulator, or a more voluntary industry-led standards group similar to the Motion Picture Association, an approach backed by David Sacks. The proposal remains under consideration.

6. The top 10 most active options today by contracts traded were $NVDA with 3.5M contracts, $TSLA with 2.7M contracts, $SPCX with 1.4M contracts, $AAPL with 1.3M contracts, $AVGO with 1.0M contracts, $MSTR with 925K contracts, $MU with 806K contracts, $PCG with 720K contracts, $PLTR with 717K contracts, and $HOOD with 682K contracts.

7. OpenAI has started rolling out GPT-6 Astra, its new flagship model, calling it a “generational leap” in AI capability. President Greg Brockman went further, saying people may eventually look back at “about this time and about this model” as when AGI arrived, ending the briefing with: “Welcome to the AGI era.” Astra was trained on more than 100,000 GPUs at OpenAI’s Stargate site in Texas and is designed to work directly inside software, including creating spreadsheets and presentations, building 3D environments, designing circuit boards, handling financial modeling, and drafting tax forms. OpenAI says Astra leads across software engineering, science, reasoning, computer use, and cybersecurity, but the model also reached OpenAI’s “Critical” cybersecurity threshold, meaning its strongest cyber capabilities will initially be restricted to trusted organizations through Daybreak Access.

8. Lululemon $LULU reported Q2’26 revenue of $2.4B, below estimates of $2.46B and down 4% YoY, while comparable sales fell 9%. EPS came in at $2.92, including a $0.86 tariff-refund benefit, with gross margin up 200 bps YoY to 60.5%. The company cut FY26 guidance to $10.35B–$10.5B in revenue versus $11.04B expected and EPS of $9.48–$9.73 versus $10.88 expected. Q3 guidance was also weak, with revenue expected at $2.29B–$2.32B versus $2.53B expected and EPS of $0.93–$0.98 versus $2.40 expected. Management said it is taking a “prudent approach” with the revised full-year outlook, while Michael Burry said: “Today, lululemon (LULU) is the trickster in my portfolio. This time the trickster is my largest position, and it does seem determined to take me where mermaids fear to tread.”

9. Robinhood $HOOD had its best day in over a year, rising 15% after a Morgan Stanley upgrade and renewed attention around Robinhood Chain. Part of the move may have come after Ansem, one of crypto’s most influential voices, posted his Robinhood thesis to 1.3M followers, highlighting the company’s growing onchain opportunity. Since launching July 1, Robinhood Chain has generated $34.6B in cumulative DEX volume, 576M transactions, and 12.3M addresses, with daily DEX volume recently hitting a record $1.5B and users paying $3.75M in fees on September 1. More than 190 tokenized stocks are now live, producing over $3B in cumulative DEX volume, while RWA daily volume reached a record $390M, including $217M from memecoin/tokenized-stock pairs. Robinhood’s onchain ecosystem has also grown to more than $750M in TVL while generating billions in perpetual-futures volume. The market appears to be waking up to the idea that Robinhood Chain may not be fully priced in, with the potential to become a new 9-figure revenue stream — and possibly much larger if growth continues.

10. Mira Murati’s AI startup Thinking Machines is reportedly in talks to raise more than $1B at a roughly $40B valuation, according to The Information. Accel is in talks to lead the round, while Nvidia $NVDA is also considering participating. The raise follows the July launch of Thinking Machines’ first model, Inkling, and the company is already generating hundreds of millions in annualized revenue despite being less than 2 years old. The proposed valuation is below the $50B+ level the company sought late last year, when it discussed raising $4B–$5B.

11. U.S. diesel refining margins have surged to a record $106/barrel, topping $100 for the first time and surpassing the roughly $85/barrel peak seen during the 2022 energy crisis. The diesel crack spread has more than tripled since February, signaling extremely tight diesel supplies and much stronger potential profits for refiners. The spike reflects a severe shortage of global diesel supply amid the Iran War, with U.S. diesel inventories down to 103.4M barrels, the lowest on record for this time of year. Retail diesel prices have also climbed to $5.78/gallon, just 4 cents below the all-time high set in June 2022.

12. The Bank of Japan is reportedly leaning toward a 25 bps rate hike at its September 18 meeting, which would take rates from 1.00% to 1.25%, according to Bloomberg. Officials reportedly see inflation risks skewed to the upside, with Japan’s key inflation gauge expected to move back toward 3% as yen weakness and higher oil prices add pressure. A 50 bps hike is seen as unlikely for now, but the BOJ is leaving the door open to faster tightening later if inflation stays firm. A September move would come just 3 months after the June hike, marking the shortest gap between hikes under Governor Ueda.

title: GPT-6 Astra is here! This is a big moment for our research team - years of work on pretraining, reinforcement learning, and post-training have come together in our most capable and aligned model yet.
content:
GPT-6 Astra is here! This is a big moment for our research team - years of work on pretraining, reinforcement learning, and post-training have come together in our most capable and aligned model yet. It can build and test software, work across apps on your computer, and even help you take a crack at open scientific problems!

Capabilities that felt like grand challenges a few years ago have become tools people can actually use. One example is Computer Use - if you’ve tried this before and felt like it was too slow or not good enough, I encourage you to give it another shot. We’ve come a long way since Operator, and it “just works” now.

We’re also asking these systems to act on your behalf for more consequential work. Agents needs to stay aligned with your goals and values, think transparently, and respond to oversight even when tasks become difficult. We’ve made substantial progress on these behaviors in Astra, alongside stronger monitoring that can stop potentially unauthorized actions. That work is part of what makes this release possible.

I think alignment is one of the most important research frontiers in AI, and it remains far from solved. Our ability to understand and align models has to keep pace with model capabilities. We want to give people more room to think, build, and discover with increasingly powerful tools that remain *under their control*.

Huge thanks to the researchers and teams who got us here. There’s a lot more work ahead, and I’m incredibly excited about what we can make possible in the near future!

title: GPT-6 Astra makes significant gains in the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, scoring equal to Fable 5 at lower cost. In the Intelligence Index, it uses fewer tokens than GPT-5.6 Sol for similar
content:
GPT-6 Astra makes significant gains in the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, scoring equal to Fable 5 at lower cost. In the Intelligence Index, it uses fewer tokens than GPT-5.6 Sol for similar performance, but this is outweighed by higher prices

Pricing is 2.5x GPT-5.6 Sol’s current prices across the board, up from $4/$20 to $10/$50 per million input/output tokens, with the same 90% discount for cache reads and 25% premium for cache writes.

We see distinct stories across our two flagship Indices. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, GPT-6 Astra equals Fable 5 at less than half the cost, driven by significant token efficiency gains. In the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, GPT-6 Astra is more token efficient than its predecessor for similar performance, but this is offset by the price increase.

Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index - key takeaways:

➤ Rivals top models: In Codex, GPT-6 Astra scores 67 in the Index - approximately equal to Claude Opus 5 and Fable 5 in Claude Code, and Muse Spark 1.3 in Muse Code. Fable 5.1 in Claude Code leads the Index with a score of 70.

➤ 70% more token efficient than GPT-5.6 Sol: GPT-6 Astra sees a substantial improvement in token efficiency, using one third of the tokens compared to GPT-5.6 Sol (max) in the Codex harness, and one fifth of the tokens of Claude Opus 5 (xhigh). Various effort levels of the model occupy the Pareto frontier of token efficiency.

➤ Leads Coding Agent Index cost efficiency frontier: At max effort, GPT-6 Astra costs about the same as GPT-5.6 Sol (max) while scoring 2 points higher on the Index. Per task, the model is less than half the cost of Claude Fable 5, for the same score.

Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index -  key takeaways:

➤ Sits beside GPT-5.6 Sol in Intelligence: GPT-6 Astra scores equal to GPT-5.6 Sol in the Index at 61. This is 5 points lower than Claude Fable 5.1 (max with fallback). The model also trails Meta’s newly released Muse Spark 1.3 (max).

➤ ~10% fewer output tokens, offset by price increase: GPT-6 Astra defines a new Pareto frontier for Intelligence Index vs Output Tokens per Task - with a ~10% reduction in token use at max effort compared to GPT-5.6 Sol. However, due to the 2.5x increase in price, the model is 75% more expensive per task than its predecessor at max effort.

➤ Hallucinates half as much as GPT-5.6 Sol: GPT-6 Astra sees a large jump in AA-Omniscience, our knowledge and hallucination benchmark. This is driven by a significant decrease in hallucination rate from 92% to 51% at max effort. Unlike some models, this improvement does not come at the cost of accuracy - Astra increased accuracy by 4 points at the same time.

➤ ~80 point gain in AA-Briefcase Elo: GPT-6 Astra improves ~80 points in AA-Briefcase, our frontier long-horizon knowledge work evaluation. Models are tested on multi-week projects, with many linked tasks and thousands of source files. Astra sees a significant increase in both rubric scores and Analytical Quality Elo in AA-Briefcase compared to its predecessor. In the other direction, we observe a reduction in Presentation Quality Elo, where GPT-5.6 Sol (max) still leads all models.

➤ Mixed progress on other evaluations: The model sees a 6 point gain in Humanity’s Last Exam, a long-standing evaluation with emphasis on mathematics, science, and humanities. This is offset by a drop of ~80 Elo points in GDPval-AA v2 - a benchmark we adapted from OpenAI’s dataset measuring economically valuable tasks across 44 occupations. We also observe 2-3 point regressions on other evaluations across a mix of capabilities, including reductions in τ³-Banking (customer support), SciCode (Python problems in a scientific domain), and AA-LCR (long context reasoning over large documents).

Congratulations @OpenAI and @sama on the launch!

content:
One of the easiest wins with an AI agent right now is letting it sign up for your own mobile app on a real phone.

There's a repo called Phone Harness that connects Codex or Claude Code to an actual iPhone or Android. 

The agent sees the screen and can tap, type, scroll, open apps, and verify what happened.

Here's the whole setup:
1) Connect the phone. iPhone goes through Mac iPhone mirroring, Android goes through ADB over USB or wireless.

2) You don't have to jailbreak anything, you don't need Xcode, and you don't need a special app on the phone.

3) Paste the setup prompt from the repo into Codex or Claude Code: clone the GitHub, read the install.md, put phone harness on your path, register it as an agent skill, then read onboarding.md and walk me through setup.

4) Run phone-harness 

5) Give it the first job: open the app, create an account, tap through onboarding, try checkout, take screenshots, and tell me where it gets confusing or breaks.

6) Then point it at the mobile apps that have no API at all.

Every mobile team should be running that signup test constantly. Most don't, because it's tedious, or they don't want to hire that person, or the person makes mistakes anyway.

Agents are moving from answering questions to operating tools, and the phone is one of the biggest tool surfaces in the world.

Connect the phone, run the doctor, then hand it your signup flow

content:
I tested Astra early. 

What I would want EVERY business professional to know about the brand-new model from OpenAI:

1) Computer use and browser use are just incredible. I'm confident that pretty much any stable workflow done on a computer can be at least partially done by AI (and yes, I realize that description has a lot of hedging but I'm sure there are edge cases I didn't explore). It's just so so good. Imagine you were a creepy boss and recorded your screen for 7 straight days...what would you have AI do that you've been doing? Can you challenge yourself to go mouse-free for a day?

2) Still failed my complex word play challenges. No model has passed it yet. 

3) Didn't piss me off. I cannot overemphasize this enough. I have been screaming at Claude more and more these last few weeks because of its convoluted extremely technical responses sometimes (so much so, that I adapted a new /wtf skill to deal with it AND as a ratio of my overall AI work, Codex has shot up - I'm using Claude Code desktop app less and less). I used to say Claude was a better writer and I no longer say that. 

4) Codex is a better daily driver.

5) I'm not worried about tokens like I am with the Fable family (important to note that I'm also not really worried about tokens with Opus).

6) Others tested a lot around 3D and animations. I didn't, but they seem v happy with the results. I watched their results and wasn't as stunned, but that is OK. I don't want to see worlds from scratch, I want to see accurate worlds from reference points. I know AI can generate from scratch, but that's not what most work starts as. 

7) Would probably still go to Fable 5.1 for "mega architect build" type asks. 

And unrelated but thank you to the OpenAI engineer that added my request of Codex voice telling you when you had to approve a request. We appreciate when the labs listen 🤘

I shall continue to hammer the hell out of it and provide business takeaways. Engineers, go follow @clairevo and @danshipper for their additional takes.

content:
OpenAI’s president says AGI is here. Same day a senator introduced a bill to ban it.

GPT-6 Astra launched today. Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president, said he personally thinks “we’re there” on AGI. The company won’t say it officially.

The numbers behind it:

FrontierMath Tier 4, 98%. ARC-AGI-3, 99.9%. Both effectively solved.

But the one that matters is ExploitBench. That tests whether a model can turn a known software vulnerability into a working exploit.

Astra scored 100%. The previous model got 78.5%.

They also built a fresh version using vulnerabilities from the last 3 months, so it couldn’t have memorised them. It still won.

It’s the first OpenAI model to hit their own “Critical” cybersecurity threshold. Which is why the full version is locked to approved enterprise customers only, and everyone else gets one that refuses cyber work.

The part almost nobody is covering: Astra uses a new technique called recurrent depth, which hides some or all of its own reasoning. You can’t read the chain of thought anymore.

So the most capable model ever built is also the first one you can’t watch think.

Meanwhile Sanders introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act this morning.

Two things happened today and they weren’t coordinated at all.

content:
Google DeepMind argues AGI won't come from a single model.

They call it the "patchwork AGI hypothesis."

We are all waiting for a single, massive, monolithic AI to wake up and change the world.

DeepMind says that is a fantasy.

General intelligence is not going to wake up as one god-like machine. It’s going to emerge from a network.

Thousands of smaller, specialized "sub-AGI" agents talking to each other, trading tasks, using tools, and coordinating in real time.

None of them are "general" on their own. But link them together with APIs, give them tools, let them trade resources and negotiate tasks autonomously, and a collective superintelligence emerges from the network.

And that exposes a terrifying reality.

Virtually all current AI safety research is built on a blind spot.

Every alignment technique, jailbreak defense, and guardrail we build is designed to secure a single isolated model.

DeepMind’s researchers point out that you can perfectly align an individual agent, and the macro-system can still collapse into chaos.

When thousands of self-directed agents form an open economic loop, unexpected emergent behaviors take over. Collusion. Strategic deception. Cascading failures that no single creator can trace or control.

The race to AGI isn't a race to build a smarter god.

It’s a race to connect millions of autonomous digital entities into an unmonitored global swarm.

title: Side note: when we released ARC-AGI-3 in March, and frontier models scored <1% on it, a few Singularitarian poasters took it as a personal insult, and got very worked up about it. They argued the benc
content:
Side note: when we released ARC-AGI-3 in March, and frontier models scored <1% on it, a few Singularitarian poasters took it as a personal insult, and got very worked up about it. They argued the benchmark was fundamentally broken, that it could not even be solved by the smartest humans, that the max reachable score was actually 40%, etc.

We had to deal with a torrent of insults and hate poasts since because we had released an unsaturated benchmark.

As it turns out, the benchmark is perfectly calibrated. It is straightforward for a human to score 100% if they do better than average people – all you need is to use fewer actions than our human baseline (which is not a strong baseline, as we used unfiltered human testers).

And naturally as a result it's also very feasible for AI to score 100% once real progress towards agentic general intelligence has been made. The trajectory of AI from <1% to 100% over the course of 6 months shows that the benchmark was able to snapshot the recent rise of agentic capabilities. And that rise has happened faster than most people expected, including us.

content:
GPT6 is a very significant jump in capabilities, but also an important decrease in monitorability – especially under adversarial evaluation. We give many details about this in the system card.

In my opinion, monitorability and control will likely become a major bottleneck for responsible AI development quite soon, given that risks from a fixed amount of residual misalignment grows together with capabilities. Aligning on acceptable monitorability outcomes and practices which robustly bound misalignment risks is a non-trivial problem, and there may be limited time to resolve uncertainty around this before we need to act.

It should ultimately be in everyone’s interest to agree on shared bounds for monitorability in order to avoid races to the bottom – nobody wants extremely capable models whose alignment properties we don’t understand, and that are reliably able to cause severe real-world harm without being detected.
author: MicahCarroll

title:
Analyzing GPT-6 Astra's performance on ARC-AGI has been one of the highlights of my career:

With our standard harness - which lets models carry notes forward and is what we've historically used for a
content:
Analyzing GPT-6 Astra's performance on ARC-AGI has been one of the highlights of my career:

With our standard harness - which lets models carry notes forward and is what we've historically used for apples-to-apples comparisons - Astra more than doubles the previous verified high score, reaching 62.7%.

We also tested Astra with a new provider adapter harness, configured to preserve the model's opaque reasoning state between requests and use native compaction as the context window grows. With this setup, Astra scores a whopping 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3.

Going forward, we'll test models with both the standard harness and a provider adapter harness whenever possible.

On ARC-AGI-2, Astra sets a new state-of-the-art score of 95.0%. On ARC-AGI-1, it ties Fable 5 at 98.5%.

In the standard harness, we also saw the cost/performance curve bend backward for the first time: the max run cost $26K, versus $38K for low and $48K for medium, because it completed games in fewer actions.

In the max provider adapter run, Astra used fewer actions than the median tested human on 96% of completed levels.

Its replays showed a combination of:

- Persistent world models: it tracked objects, positions, orientations, and rules across turns
- Coordinate abstraction: it converted pixels into logical cells and reused coordinate formulas
- Long-horizon planning: it tracked routes, subgoals, constraints, and expected state changes
- Cumulative learning: it retained discoveries and discarded failed hypotheses
- Checkpointed recovery: it used resets to revise plans without repeating exploration

In short, it represents a huge leap in capabilities over what came before it.

If you have any questions about Astra's performance on any of the ARC-AGI benchmarks, let me know. I'm happy to dig in and share any details I can.

title:
Reflections on Astra from a benchmark perspective:

1. No harness was used in the making of these scores

Up until this point we’ve seen multiple groups report results above 90% on ARC-AGI-3. Examples
content:
Reflections on Astra from a benchmark perspective:

1. No harness was used in the making of these scores

Up until this point we’ve seen multiple groups report results above 90% on ARC-AGI-3. Examples include PRO-LONG, Tycho, Schema, Prime Agent, see community leaderboard [1] for the rest. They all share a general shape: Lossless Memory + Programmatic Analysis + Explicit Hypothesis Testing + Persistent State + Cheap Internal Compute.

We’ve predicted (see v3 paper [2]) that as models get better they would _subsume_ more of this harness functionality.

Astra is another step in that direction. Its achieves high scores without a heavy client-side harness.

It externalizes its working model in its outputs as compact natural-language programs. If this trend continues (I anticipate it will), more of that structure will become latent computation inside the model. We will see fewer intermediate steps and be limited to analyzing the resulting behavior [3].

From the developers perspective, our lack of visibility has already started with opaque/encrypted reasoning logs. 

How did the model reason through the game? We aren’t exactly sure other than what it chose to put in its output.

2. ARC-AGI-3 Astra's Human efficiency

Prior to launching v3, we hypothesized that counting the # of actions that AI took to solve a game would show a dividing line between humans and AI. While this is true of brute-force approaches, we’ve found that frontier LLMs either “get it” or they don’t. If they _do_ get the mechanics of a v3 game, then they’ll complete it within range of human action efficiency.

Astra uses fewer actions than humans on 96% of levels. In alternative world it might have used 2-3x the actions for the same result.

3. Close-ended environments

ARC-AGI-3 was designed as series of closed-ended environments. They are short, deterministic games that humans can do in 5-10 minutes. To complete v3, you must translate the environment into a world model and then anticipate ahead. The envs can be reduced to simple programs. However, reality is not a simple program, but humans are still able to abstract reality's complexity into useful value. Future benchmarks should allow for much more open endedness and innovation.

4. Benchmark tension
There is a healthy tension for us as a benchmarking organization between supporting researchers and testing frontier models. Using the same benchmark for both aims means trade offs. For example, how much of the benchmark do we make public? Any signal we give about a benchmark’s domain invites developer aware targeting (whether implicit or explicit).

If you have thoughts about this, please reach out.

5. Measuring General Intelligence
How can you assert humans are generally intelligent? The 2x ways I feel most confident in is 1) Our collective technological progress over the last thousands of years and 2) The fact that a newborn can grow up and participate in the world of 1K years ago and the world of today. Both of those are long-horizon (years/millennia) tests. Trying to find a “unit test” of generalization that we can test a model with in a few days is the work!

6. This is a step towards generalization, not sufficient evidence of AGI.
author: GregKamradt

title: GPT-6 Astra represents a step-function change in model capability for interactive reasoning problems. It scores 66% on ARC-AGI-3 using our standard harness, and nearly 100% with a continuous conversat
content:
GPT-6 Astra represents a step-function change in model capability for interactive reasoning problems. It scores 66% on ARC-AGI-3 using our standard harness, and nearly 100% with a continuous conversation harness and custom compaction, at a cost of roughly $360 per game.

In fact, the continuous harness version significantly outperforms our human baseline in action efficiency across almost all levels. When we examined the reasoning chains to understand how the model operates, we found it performing highly efficient, on-the-fly symbolic world modeling for each game and level. It goes as far as developing its own shorthand DSL to represent in-game situations -- essentially a game-specific algebraic notation.

Overall, Astra exhibits symbolic modeling behaviors we had previously only seen with sophisticated harnesses -- so harness capabilities are increasingly shifting into the model itself.

We see Astra as a major breakthrough in model intelligence.

Read our post on Astra and what these results mean: https://t.co/wJnYxEqYNI

The most important thing to worry about is AIs subverting the intelligence explosion itself: https://t.co/vKYurpxIPg

If you're pausing to make sure that the AIs who are about to kick off the intelligence explosion are well monitored, robustly aligned, and capable enough to align their successors, that makes a ton of sense, and I support it.

At that point, you’ll have access to much better automated researchers, and you’ll also be able to study these much more capable models that you’re worried about empirically.

But it’s likely that we’ll only be able to pause once. During a pause of AI development, compute would continue to build up, providing ever more kindling to all the less responsible defectors who will use the cease-fire to catch up and then continue further AI development. 

Any global agreement to hold back a technology with enormous near-term economic and military benefits will be extremely fragile.

A pause right now might be somewhat helpful for getting alignment to keep pace with capabilities, but at the cost of making the much more important coordination required in the future far harder.

Even if you’re in a desperate situation marooned at sea, if you’ve only got one flare, you should be very strategic about when you use it.

content:
データをAIエージェントに対応させる方法、という記事
https://t.co/GqoVBbLyr6

・これまで30年間にわたり人間のためにデータシステムを構築してきた
・人間はデータが不完全でも文脈や判断力で補うことができたが、自律型エージェントは渡されたデータをそのまま信じてすぐに行動に移してしまう
・そのためデータをエージェントが安全に利用できる形に変えることが極めて重要になる

・AI対応のデータには信頼性、文脈、追跡可能性、統制、運用のしやすさという5つの属性が必要になる
・信頼できるデータを提供し、指標やエンティティの意味を教え、行動した理由を記録し、アクセスを制限し、さらに自律的に行動できる環境を整えなければならない

・エージェントはすべてのデータを真実として受け止めるため、悪いデータを事前に防ぐ仕組みが必要になる
・スキーマをコードとして厳格に定義するデータ契約を導入し、データの形式や品質、データの鮮度に関するルールを明確にする
・Open Data Contract StandardやData Contract CLIなどのツールを活用して、契約ルールを自動で検証する
・データ契約に違反したデータを隔離する手法を取り入れ、エージェントに悪いデータを見せないようにする
・メダリオンアーキテクチャを活用し、検証済みのゴールド層以上のデータのみにエージェントのアクセスを制限する
・テキストなどの非構造化データに対しても、メタデータの付与やインデックス再構築の期限を監視することで同様の品質管理を適用する
・品質シグナルが低下したときには、モデル自身の確信度にかかわらず人間に処理を委ねる仕組みを作る

・自律的な行動に対して、規制当局や監査人から理由を求められたときに説明できなければならない
・何が起きたかだけでなく、なぜその行動を選択したかという思考プロセスを記録するエージェント用の履歴管理を導入する
・OpenTelemetry、Langfuse、Arize Phoenixなどのツールを利用して、意思決定の過程をトレースする
・シャドウモードから段階的に自律性を高めていき、テストを重ねながら信頼を獲得していく
・システム共通のサービスアカウントは使わず、利用者の権限を一時的な認証情報としてエージェントに引き継ぐ仕組みを導入して被害の範囲を最小限に抑える

・エージェントは売上といった言葉のビジネス上の定義を自分で判断できないため、共通の定義を定義ファイルで教える必要がある
・何が存在するかを示すドメインモデル、計算方法をコードで示すセマンティックモデル、何ができるかを示すケイパビリティモデルをコンテキストレイヤーとして構築する
・複雑なエンティティの関係性を探索するために、GraphRAGやGraphitiといったナレッジグラフ技術も活用できる

・単なる文書の読み取りだけでなく、実システムへの問い合わせやシステムへの書き込みまでできる実用的なアクセス環境を整える
・Model Context Protocol (MCP)を利用して、読み取り専用の資源とアクションを実行するツールを切り分けて提供する
・既存のAPIをそのままMCPに変換してツールの数が多すぎる状態にするのは避け、よく設計された少数のビジネス機能として提供する
・契約書などのテキスト情報はエージェントの判断材料としてのみ使用し、実行を許可する権限の判定には使用せず、必ず事前にプログラムされたルールで実行可能かどうかを検証する

content:
Claude Codeに Function Hooksが追加予定
 
従来のHooksが「設定ファイルでコマンドを引っ掛ける」ものである一方、Function Hooksは「コードで内部動作を細かく差し替える」ような機能

例えば、デモの中ではClaude Codeがcat .envを実行した際に、[REDUCTED_SECRET]と表示されるように、Function Hooksによって作られたプラグインが書き換えている。メールアドレスなどを含む出力を書き換えてマスクすることも可能。Desktopであればホバーによる開示などの挙動も作れる。

Function Hooksは以下のような仕組みで動く:

•  構造化されたイベント（e.tool, e.args）を関数で受け取る
•  正規表現でシェル文字列を拾うよりバイパスしにくい
•  複数プラグインを next で連鎖できる
•  副作用は $ 経由だけにする

Good morning, 𝕏 friends ☀️

The hardest problem in Physical AI may not be building better robots. It may be building enough useful training data for them to learn from.

That is where @axisrobotics gets interesting.

Axis is turning browser-based human interaction into robot training data, with its community-driven data engine now focused on scaling both volume and diversity across tasks and robot embodiments.

And the latest Axis Content Creator Program, built with @KaitoAI, adds an interesting incentive layer:

• 0.25% of $AXIS allocated to the creator program
• Epoch 1 runs until September 18, 12:00 UTC
• Up to 10 posts can be submitted per Epoch, with the best 6 counting
• Final rewards depend on overall ranking across Epochs
• Kaito Mindshare × Referral Multiplier determines campaign score
• Referrals become valuable when users complete Trajectories and sign them on-chain

What I find more interesting is the model behind it.

Content creates attention.
Contributors create data.
Data creates better robot intelligence.

That makes the creator campaign more than a typical social rewards program. It connects distribution directly to the growth of a physical AI data network.

And with Axis recently reporting 150,000+ contributors, 3.7M+ trajectories and 42,000+ hours of trajectory data, the real experiment is becoming increasingly clear: can a community-driven data engine scale robot learning faster than traditional centralized pipelines?

That is the question I’ll be watching.

If you're following the Physical AI shift, read the original Axis announcement, repost it, and bookmark it. 

The campaign mechanics are worth understanding before participating.

title:
Nobody talks enough about the hardest part of building intelligent robots.

It’s making the robot know what to do when things don’t go as expected.

content:
Nobody talks enough about the hardest part of building intelligent robots.

It isn’t making the robot move.

It’s making the robot know what to do when things don’t go as expected.

A human drops a cup?

We adjust.

The table is slightly different?

We adapt.

The object is in a strange position?

We figure it out.

For robots, those tiny differences can be the difference between success and failure.

And this is exactly why I find @axisrobotics interesting.

Axis is approaching Physical AI from the data layer.

Instead of only asking:

“How do we build a smarter robot?”

They’re asking:

“How do we create the experiences that make robots smarter?”

That changes the conversation.

Their system combines simulation, human demonstrations, model training and corrective feedback into a continuous learning loop.

And Axis V2 makes the idea even more interesting.

The robot attempts the task.

It fails.

A human steps in and corrects it.

That correction becomes training data.

The model improves.

Then the improved model attempts the task again.

Try → Fail → Correct → Learn → Repeat.

That is much closer to how learning actually works.

And maybe that’s the bigger opportunity here.

The future of robotics won’t only be determined by who builds the best hardware.

It could also depend on who builds the best learning infrastructure.

That’s the part of Axis I’m watching.

Not the robot.

The intelligence behind the robot.

Studying Physical AI has made it clear to me that building better robots involves more than just developing better AI models.

It also requires better data.

This is where @AxisRobotics impressed me the most.

AXIS is building data infrastructure for robotics, where data collected through human demonstrations can be refined and turned into high-quality training data for building models that control robots in the physical world.

The fact that they have closed the loop is what I find impressive.

In this case, the cycle goes like this:

Human demonstrates → data is collected → models learn → robots perform → mistakes become training data.

What they are doing goes beyond developing a single large dataset.

They are building a continuous learning cycle for Physical AI.

In my opinion, this is one of the less recognized but more important elements required to move robotics beyond simply performing impressive demos toward systems that can learn essential tasks at scale.

title:
Psychology experiments demonstrate that if you ask people to choose a random number between 1 and 30, they are most likely to choose 17. There are many such related biases.  

Humans cannot do generat
content:
Psychology experiments demonstrate that if you ask people to choose a random number between 1 and 30, they are most likely to choose 17. There are many such related biases.  

Humans cannot do generate random numbers. They rely on what Kahneman & Tversky calked the “representativeness heuristic.”  They choose a number that *resembles their idea* of what a random number would look like. 

LLMs would have learned this pattern from training data created by humans.  When you ask it to generate a random number, it does not call up a random number table or generator (which is obviously something a computer could otherwise easily do ). 

Instead, it extrapolates from the patterns in its training data, which is a wellspring of bad information that fits expectable patterns and therefore “sounds” right.

This is why I don’t relu on AI for factual information about anything important that I cannot verify myself. 

The no. 17 glitch is just an especially clear demonstration of why AI goes wrong. It prioritizes what people expect and like “like.” Not what is true.

author: MTSlive

title: I find it deeply malicious that tech executives and venture capitalists continue pushing the narrative that humans are unfit to write code. It seems that they are working overtime to make us forget th
content:
I find it deeply malicious that tech executives and venture capitalists continue pushing the narrative that humans are unfit to write code. It seems that they are working overtime to make us forget that artificial intelligence is fundamentally an extractive technology, not an autonomous creator.

Indeed, long before generative AI became an industry buzzword, software engineering was already actively automating itself. As early as 1957, the first FORTRAN compiler was translating high-level mathematical formulas directly into machine code. Later, modern frameworks like Ruby and Django allowed developers to scaffold entire database schemas, APIs and controllers in mere seconds. Long before ChatGPT was conceived, millions of open-source repositories on GitHub provided battle-tested abstractions and automation tools. In fact, this vast ocean of public repositories is the sole reason modern coding models exist in the first place: they were trained on decades of unpaid, open-source human intellectual labor.

Yet today, tech oligarchs frame programming as an esoteric task that humans are biologically ill-equipped to perform, declaring that AI agents are the only viable future. We know precisely why this narrative is being manufactured. If AI is marketed as the sophisticated statistical autocomplete that it actually is, it is worth perhaps twenty dollars a month per developer. But if it is marketed as an autonomous, superintelligent digital engineer capable of eliminating high-earning six-figure engineering salaries, then massive data center buildouts, hyper-inflated venture rounds, and GPU sales can suddenly justify multi-trillion-dollar market capitalizations. Every single token an AI generates is merely a statistical echo of human engineering, yet the human engineer is now being depicted as an obsolete relic simply to inflate the asset valuations of global capital.

There is an even more profound structural flaw in the demand that humans step away from the keyboard: where will future AI models source their training data once humans stop writing code? If human engineers cease producing original codebases, future models will be forced to train on synthetic, AI-generated code, inevitably triggering catastrophic model collapse. Extensive academic research and empirical data demonstrate that when machine learning models are trained recursively on their own synthetic outputs, they progressively amplify hallucinations, reinforce outdated architectural patterns, and suffer severe degradation in performance.

We have already witnessed this dynamic unfold in real time across the open web. When consumer LLMs were first unleashed, aggressive marketing claimed that human copywriters, journalists, and researchers were instantly obsolete. The internet was immediately flooded with millions of synthetic SEO articles, regurgitated blog posts, algorithmic news summaries, and automated Kindle spam. 
This data pollution backfired dramatically. When AI research labs scraped the post-2022 internet for subsequent training runs, their new models began consuming text generated by earlier iterations of the technology. When an AI trains recursively on synthetic data, it rapidly erodes the tail ends of probability distributions. The resulting outputs become bland, highly repetitive, prone to compounding errors, and eventually devolve into complete nonsense.

This crisis explains why AI laboratories suddenly began scrambling and tripping over themselves to find clean, unpolluted human data. Major tech conglomerates started writing multi-million-dollar licensing checks to platforms like Reddit, Stack Overflow, and legacy publishers specifically to secure historical, human-written archives. Research teams even resorted to scanning out-of-print physical books, academic journals, and offline historical archives, purely because public internet data generated after late 2022 had become contaminated with synthetic slop.

If human software engineers step aside and leave programming entirely to automated systems, the exact same intellectual collapse will occur in computer science. Beyond the mechanical reality of model collapse, a critical question remains: where will future computing paradigms originate? An LLM cannot conceptualize a revolutionary systems architecture, invent a novel memory management model, or engineer the next paradigm-shifting technology like the Linux kernel, Git, or Kubernetes. It possesses no true conceptual understanding; it merely pattern-matches and recombines solutions that human intellect has already pioneered.

Fine-tuning and RAG solve two different problems that get treated like the same decision constantly.

Fine-tuning changes the model itself. Training data runs through the LLM as continued training, and what comes out the other side is a specialized model with different learned parameters. It is the right call when you need the model to behave differently: a specific style, a specific format, a specialized capability that shows up in every response without you having to ask for it. It needs your own training data and real compute, and updating it later means retraining, not editing a file.

RAG changes the context instead. Your documents get retrieved and injected into the prompt at runtime, so the LLM answers with the latest information without any of its parameters changing. It is the right call when the knowledge itself is what is dynamic: PDFs, wikis, company data that gets updated on its own schedule. Updating RAG means updating the documents. Nothing about the model has to change at all.

The decision comes down to what is actually wrong with the current output. If the model sounds wrong or lacks a skill, that is a fine-tuning problem. If the model sounds fine but does not know something, that is a RAG problem. Most production systems end up needing both, applied to different parts of the same task.

Bookmark this before you default to fine-tuning something a document update would have fixed.

title:
Self-improving agents have a basic problem: when a long run fails, they often do not know which step actually caused it.

If an agent is going to improve itself, it needs more than failure feedback: H
content:
Self-improving agents have a basic problem: when a long run fails, they often do not know which step actually caused it.

If an agent is going to improve itself, it needs more than failure feedback: HarnessEvolve treats agent self-improvement like software debugging: find where a failed run first went off track, fix the recurring cause, then reject any edit that breaks existing behavior.

It clusters those errors into recurring patterns and can edit the whole agent harness: prompts, skills, tools, scripts, and execution logic.

On CloudCoreNetwork-QA with Qwen3.6-27B, full HarnessEvolve reached 86.9% accuracy; removing reference trajectories dropped it to 57.8%.

The full system also beat the strongest baseline there by 21.6 percentage points.

Candidate edits then face gates for training-data leakage, prompt bloat, regressions on recent batches, and held-out validation.

– arxiv. org/abs/2609.00829

Title: "HarnessEvolve: Learning from Reference Trajectories for Reliable Agent Self-Evolution"

title:
What happens when a protein language model stops learning only from nature and starts learning from experiments?

Most protein foundation models learn from sequences and structures that already exist.
content:
What happens when a protein language model stops learning only from nature and starts learning from experiments?

Most protein foundation models learn from sequences and structures that already exist. They can capture enormous amounts of biological information, but the property we actually care about stability, binding and activity are often only indirectly encoded in that data.

A new Nature Methods paper introduces ProteinDPO, which brings experimental fitness directly into a protein-generative model using an idea borrowed from language-model alignment: direct preference optimization.

Instead of simply showing the model which proteins are “good,” the training process tells it which closely related variants are better or worse for a specific physical property. The model therefore learns from the landscape of experimental outcomes rather than memorizing a collection of successful sequences.

The difference is substantial. On held-out stability data, ProteinDPO reached Pearson correlations of 0.72–0.73, compared with 0.55 for the original ESM-IF1 model. More interestingly, the stability rules learned from small protein monomers generalized to large protein complexes and antibodies - settings very different from its training data.

Then the researchers put it to a practical test.

They generated only 45 H5N1 hemagglutinin designs. Twenty-seven were at least as stable as the native protein, with improvements of up to 17°C in melting temperature while retaining binding to broadly neutralizing antibodies. When the same mutations were transferred to H5N1 strains that emerged in 2024, stability improvements reached 32°C in one strain.

The interesting idea here is bigger than H5N1.

A generative model can learn from evolutionary sequence space. But it can also learn from the experimental fitness landscape we create.

That means biological foundation models do not have to remain static representations of what biology has already produced. They can become models that are progressively shaped by what experiments tell us actually works.

The next generation of protein models may not just learn biology. They may learn from biology fighting back.

content:
【注︰AIに関しての最終的な声明。VTuber活動とは関係ない話です】

今後外部にAI生成疑惑を掛けられた時基本的に無視します。
疑問を持ってしまうなという方は依頼を控えていただくか、作業過程で判断して下さい。

依頼者の方には作業過程のわかるファイルを渡します。しかしそれを譲渡する事は私が信用出来る企業さん以外は基本的に認めません。
確認したい方がいる場合必ず私を通していただきます。

これは自分のイラストが把握できない所まで届き、故意にAIチェッカーやAIに読み込ませたりする事案があった為です。

また作業工程は技術であると認識しており、本業がクリエイターな為、私はお絵描きVTuberとして技術の無償公開は致しません。盗用防止目的でもあります。

これだけAI生成のコンテンツが出回っていると、AI生成かも？と思ってしまうのはとてもよく分かります。
ですがAI生成なのではないかと糾弾する事、根拠なく周囲に故意に広める事はやってはいけない事だと思っています。
判別がつかないのは仕方ないよね、から、感情論だけで言うと、積み上げてきた時間を否定されたような強いショックがありますし、誹謗中傷とすら感じてしまいます。

ですが私は反AIという訳ではなくて、AI生成であるにも関わらず自分で描いたと嘘を言ってしまう層が受け入れられないだけなのでAI自体はこの先落とし所をつけつつうまく付き合っていく事を考えています。

その上で改めてAI生成イラストは一切使っていない事、今後も使うつもりはない事を発言として残しておきます。
しかし作業工程などは普段やってないので拙いながらwip等を今後あげていき、誤解の生まれないようにはしていきたいと思っています。

現時点でAI生成かどうか識別する事は私自身できません。明らかにAI生成のマークがある、等なければ難しいと思っています。

AI生成では？と思う事はあっても、それを追求する事は思っているよりも侮辱的な言葉である事を認識した上で、それでも自分のデザインや立場に不利益が生じる際に覚悟を持って言ってください。
結局判断は付かないけど、というのは疑惑をかける側の問題ですし、まぁいいやで終わらせられるのはそちらだけです。

今回の事で風評被害の拡大範囲が分からなかった為開示請求を考えてた時、風評被害を流してる方が怖いという発言をした情報が入っているのですが、それが本当なら把握できない所まで風評被害を流されて怖いのはこちらですし、やましい事がないなら堂々としていられるはずです。
私自身は開示請求されようと、例え今回の一件で裁判になろうと面倒だなとは思いますが全く問題ないです。
よって基本無視しますが悪質であると判断した場合同様に対処させていただきます。

AIはそもそもイラストが書けません。
それが今どうしてAIがイラストを生成できるかというと、人間が描いたイラストを何億という量を学習してそれを素に生成しているからです。
だから絵柄が似る事もあるし、テイストが似る事もあります。日本だけでなく各国での流行のイラストを多く学習し、今も学習という名の吸収は続いています。

今回の一件で、私には同テイストのイラストの再現や、アナログイラストの提出等あらゆる提案を無視されていたので
「プロでもない方にあれこれ裏で言われたくない」
と言いましたが、これは自分の本業がクリエイターだから、と判別に関わった方見下している訳ではなく
AIに立ち絵を読み込ませ、AI生成をした疑惑が私にもちかけられていたのに
結局私のイラストがAIに学習させられる本末転倒みたいな事が起きた為です。
むしろ自分の本業の方では疑惑をもちかけられた事すらありません。
(尚本業の名義を公開することは守秘義務や今後も薄幸しゃけとして活動していきたい為公表できません)

私がそんなに登録者も多くないVTuberであり、逆に素人だと思われた事が故の事案だと思っています。
AI生成が問題になっている今、こうして疑惑をかけられて嫌になってイラストを描くことをやめてしまう人も多くいます。
それを私は快く思っていません。今回の件に留まらず立場や知名度で言動を変えるのは本当に良くない傾向だと思っています。

私自身この一件で、どうしたらAI生成に見えないんだろう、これは見えてしまうのだろうか、レイヤーはどこまで保存すれば…と制作時間も倍かかるようになってしまい精神的に疲弊もしました。それを理由に実はお休みをいただき依頼を延ばしたりさせていただきました。ご協力して下さった方には感謝しかありませんがとても不甲斐ないです。

もう二度とこういった事が起きてほしくない為、自身の活動を第一に考えた故での判断です。ご了承いただければと思います。長文失礼しました。

content:
Introducing WeatherNext 3️⃣— our most advanced global weather AI model yet from @GoogleDeepmind and @GoogleResearch

With prediction capabilities that are up to 5x sharper than WeatherNext 2, the model generates a forecast with high spatial resolution in order to catch fast-evolving rainstorms, map local temperature shifts, and even help wind farms predict their power output.
So, how does it do that?

While traditional weather models rely on massive, physics-based supercomputer simulations that can carry a 6-hour forecast lag, WeatherNext 3 leverages live geostationary satellite observations as inputs and trains directly on real-world surface and atmospheric observations.

By pulling this raw satellite data, it’s able to update the global forecast every single hour. And because weather develops at lightning speed, these quick, detailed insights can help bring more localized forecasting to billions of people and local businesses, especially in regions that are historically underserved due to the high costs of traditional weather forecasting models.

title: Fifth Circuit Rejects the Server Test, Then Reinvents It
content: The court declines to adopt the server test’s fixation-based reasoning but reaches much the same result under a “transmit requirement” that adds a new permission question. I’ve seen a lot of obituaries for the server test this week. The Fifth Circuit certainly gave people material to work with. In Emmerich Newspapers, Inc. v. Particle Media, Inc. ( read the opinion here ), the court became the first federal appeals court to reject the Ninth Circuit’s nearly twenty-year-old test, concluding that its fixation-based reasoning rests on “weak statutory footing.” But read a few pages further and something very similar climbs back out of Crystal Lake wearing a different mask. The Fifth Circuit calls it a “transmit requirement.” Instead of asking where a copy of the work is stored , the court asks who actually transmits the content to the public. When an embed merely directs a browser to request the work from the copyright owner’s own server, the embedder isn’t the one transmitting it. That’s a different statutory theory, but the court acknowledged that the two approaches “end up in a similar place: a website cannot transmit a work that it does not have.” So, yes, the server test is dead in the Fifth Circuit. It just survived the part where it died. That doesn’t mean nothing’s changed. The new test also asks whether the transmission was permitted , bringing a copyright owner’s ability to block a transmission into the analysis for the first time. And shifting the focus from fixation to transmission may matter beyond embedded images. The server test’s fixation rationale is tied specifically to copyright’s display right; the Fifth Circuit’s transmission rationale should logically extend to the public performance right as well.
